title: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management
text:
4.1 A fifth dimension of the system of objectives
In Chapter 3 we depicted the logistics system of objectives as a tetrahedron: quality, speed, cost and flexibility/resilience form four vertices between which every logistics system has to position itself, because an improvement at one vertex almost always comes at the expense of at least one other. This view was deliberately limited to the classic performance dimensions of logistics – that is, the variables by which supply chains have primarily been measured for decades.
For some years now, this system of objectives has been joined by a further, independent dimension that cannot be fitted seamlessly into any of the four vertices of the tetrahedron and is therefore treated separately in this chapter: sustainability. Sustainability is not a “fifth vertex” that simply sits alongside the other four, but a cross-cutting dimension that affects each of the four original vertices – cost (e.g. through carbon pricing or investment in low-emission vehicles), speed (e.g. when a lower-emission rail connection takes longer than the lorry), quality (e.g. through requirements for recycled materials) and flexibility (e.g. when take-back systems tie up additional capacity). Anyone who takes sustainability in supply chain management seriously must therefore follow the same trade-off logic we have already encountered for the classic tetrahedron – except that an additional objective, often difficult to monetise, now enters the trade-off.
This chapter addresses this dimension. It deepens the sustainability content of the lecture unit “Objectives, trade-offs and logistics costs” and therefore follows directly on from Chapter 3. We first clarify what sustainability actually means in the SCM context, then examine how companies can respond strategically to environmental requirements, systematise the multitude of environmental SCM strategies in a hierarchy, turn to the circular economy as a central design principle and finally use our own R calculation to investigate how the central trade-off between sustainability and the classic logistics objectives can be quantified using a concrete example – the choice of transport mode.
crumbs: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management

title: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management
section: 4.2 What does sustainability mean in supply chain management?
text:
4.2 What does sustainability mean in supply chain management?
The term “sustainability” is used so inflationarily today that a clear definition is essential before we apply it to supply chains. The most influential definition to this day comes from the United Nations’ Brundtland Report, published in 1987:

Definition: Sustainability
A social system is described as sustainable if it can be regarded as both intragenerationally and intergenerationally just. Just means that it “meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs” (Hauff 1987).

Two aspects of this definition deserve particular attention. First, it refers to intragenerational justice – that is, justice within the generation living today, for instance between industrialised and developing countries or between different population groups. Second, it refers to intergenerational justice – justice between present and future generations. From the outset, sustainability is therefore not a purely environmental concept but explicitly a social and economic one as well: resources must not be consumed today in such a way that future generations can no longer meet their own needs, and this constraint applies equally to natural, social and economic “resources”.
From this combination of economic, environmental and social aspects emerged the most widespread classification scheme in sustainability management: the triple bottom line (Baumast and Pape 2013). It distinguishes three equally ranked target dimensions whose joint fulfilment – not the one-sided maximisation of a single dimension – is regarded as sustainable:

the economic dimension: lasting competitiveness, profitability and value creation – ultimately the classic objectives that we have already discussed in detail in Chapter 3,
the environmental dimension: conserving natural resources, avoiding and reducing emissions and maintaining the functioning of ecosystems,
the social dimension: decent working conditions along the entire supply chain, health protection, equal opportunities and social participation.

From this, a workable working definition for supply chain management can be derived, which guides this chapter:

Definition: Sustainable supply chain management
Sustainable supply chain management (sustainable SCM) refers to the planning, execution and control of business processes taking into account economic, environmental and social objectives in order to ensure the long-term competitiveness of the supply chain (Bouchery et al. 2016).

What is remarkable about this definition is that it does not frame sustainability as the opposite of competitiveness, but as its prerequisite: a supply chain that ignores its environmental and social impacts risks reputational damage, regulatory intervention, rising raw material prices and the loss of market access – and thus ultimately precisely the economic competitiveness it actually wanted to protect by neglecting sustainability. Sustainability and classic SCM objectives therefore stand in a dual relationship: in the short term often in conflict (more sustainability usually costs money or time at first), but complementary in the long term (a lack of sustainability jeopardises competitiveness itself).

section: 4.3 The environmental strategic fit: how companies respond to environmental requirements
text:
4.3 The environmental strategic fit: how companies respond to environmental requirements
Not every company is affected by environmental issues to the same extent, and not every company responds equally offensively to a given level of exposure. To systematise this observation, a two-dimensional grid can be constructed – analogous to the strategic fit concept from Chapter 2 (Günther 2008):

the company’s environmental exposure (low to high): How strongly does business success depend on natural resources, emission regulations or environmental reputational risks?
the company’s environmental orientation (low to high): How actively does the company position itself strategically on environmental issues?

Combining the two dimensions yields four ideal-typical positions, summarised in the following table:

The axes are to be read such that the upper half of the grid (high exposure) comprises companies that can hardly escape environmental requirements – they respond either defensively (resistance) or adaptively (adaptation). In the lower half (low exposure), by contrast, there is a choice: environmental issues can be ignored or used offensively as a differentiating feature, even though there is no immediate pressure. The four positions thus show that exposure alone does not determine a strategy: SKW Piesteritz and EON are both highly exposed to environmental issues because of their industry, but respond to them very differently – the one in a minimalist, wait-and-see manner (environmental resistance), the other by actively transforming its own business model (environmental adaptation). This has an important consequence for supply chain management: a company’s own position in the grid directly influences which of the strategies presented below are seriously considered at all – an environmentally offensive company will be more willing to invest in circular product design or remanufacturing than an environmentally resistant one.

title: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management
section: 4.4 From rules of action to concepts: a hierarchy of environmental SCM strategies
text:
4.4 From rules of action to concepts: a hierarchy of environmental SCM strategies
In practice there is an almost unmanageable variety of individual measures with which companies respond to environmental requirements – from route optimisation and recycling rates to car sharing. To provide orientation within this variety, a four-level hierarchy model of environmentally oriented business can be constructed, ranging from very general rules of action to concrete concepts that can be implemented directly (Dyckhoff et al. 2008). The logic of this hierarchy is deductive: rules of action justify basic strategies, basic strategies are operationalised through basic principles, and basic principles finally lead to concrete concepts that can actually be implemented in individual companies.
At the top level are four rules of action, which formulate the conditions under which economic activity can be regarded as environmentally sustainable: keeping ecological systems healthy (e.g. IKEA’s certified timber sourcing), respecting the absorptive capacity of ecological systems (e.g. emissions monitoring in chemical parks based on pollution limits), balanced use of renewable resources (e.g. fishing quotas based on the reproductive capacity of stocks) and balanced use of non-renewable resources (e.g. aluminium recycling to conserve primary raw materials). These four rules translate the abstract Brundtland definition into concrete requirements for dealing with natural systems.
From these rules of action, three basic strategies can be derived, often also referred to as the “three big S” of environmental strategy: sufficiency aims at lower absolute resource consumption through less, slower or more needs-based consumption – for instance when Patagonia deliberately promotes repairs instead of new purchases, or when sharing models encourage the collective rather than individual use of products. Efficiency means achieving the same or a higher output with less energy and material input – for instance through route optimisation in logistics or the conversion of store networks to LED lighting, which requires significantly less electricity for the same lighting output. Consistency, finally, seeks to design material and energy flows to be compatible with nature from the outset, for instance through closed material loops (Interface for carpet tiles) or the replacement of fossil energy sources with renewable ones. The difference between these three strategies is important: sufficiency reduces consumption in absolute terms, efficiency reduces it relative to the output delivered, and consistency changes the type of material and energy flows used without necessarily reducing their quantity.
At the third level are four basic principles, which describe how companies implement the basic strategies organisationally. The responsibility principle requires those who cause environmental impacts to also take responsibility for their consequences – for instance within the framework of extended producer responsibility for packaging or systematic carbon accounting that attributes emissions to a company’s own value creation. The cooperation principle assumes that environmental problems can be solved better through collaboration than through isolated individual action, for instance in the form of industry initiatives for sustainable supply chains or industrial symbiosis, in which the waste heat or by-products of one plant are used by another. The circularity principle calls for materials to be kept in circulation for as long as possible – a principle to which we devote the next section in detail. And the principle of function orientation places the desired function rather than the physical product at the centre: car sharing sells mobility instead of vehicle ownership, “light as a service” sells lighting instead of a stock of lamps.
Finally, at the lowest and most concrete level are four concepts with which companies implement the basic principles in day-to-day business: dematerialisation replaces material processes with digital solutions (digital instead of printed invoices, streaming instead of physical media); increasing energy efficiency delivers the same output with less energy input (heat recovery in production); decoupling breaks problematic links between economic growth and resource consumption (working from home instead of commuting, regional instead of global sourcing); and deceleration relies on slower, longer-lasting usage patterns (slow fashion instead of short collection cycles, rail instead of air for business travel). The following table summarises this four-level hierarchy with one practical example each.

title: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management
section: 4.5 Planning tasks in sustainable supply chain management
text:
4.5 Planning tasks in sustainable supply chain management
Sustainability changes not only the objectives but also the planning tasks along the supply chain. Stindt (2017) classifies these – analogous to the supply chain planning matrix from Chapter 5 – by planning level and process. At the strategic level, the focus is on designing a network that can accommodate return flows (take-back, reprocessing, recycling) in addition to forward flows, on selecting suppliers according to environmental and social criteria and on designing products for circularity. At the tactical level, capacities for return and reprocessing are dimensioned, transport modes are chosen with emissions in mind and emission budgets are allocated to sites and periods. Finally, at the operational level, the focus is on low-emission route planning, the control of returns and the avoidance of spoilage and waste in day-to-day business.
Stindt’s central thesis is that sustainability cannot be “bolted on” as an additional, downstream planning module but must be integrated into existing planning tasks: each of the models covered in this course reader – facility location planning, the transportation problem, inventory planning – can be extended with environmental objectives or constraints, as already indicated in Chapter 3 with CO₂ prices and emission budgets.
crumbs: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management

title: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management
section: 4.6 From the linear to the circular supply chain
text:
4.6 From the linear to the circular supply chain
Of the four basic principles in the previous section, the circularity principle deserves closer examination because it changes the structure of entire supply chains – not just individual processes within an unchanged chain logic. To understand this structural change, it is worth first looking at the waste hierarchy of the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, which ranks the fundamentally available ways of dealing with materials and products at the end of their life cycle according to environmental preferability:

Codetibble(
  Rang = 1:6,
  Stufe = c("Prevent", "Reduce", "Reuse", "Recycling", "Energy Recovery", "Disposal"),
  Bedeutung = c(
    "Avoid the generation of waste in the first place (e.g. through sufficiency or function orientation)",
    "Reduce the amount of material used (efficiency)",
    "Continue to use products or components without further processing",
    "Reprocess material and use it again as a raw material",
    "Use material that can no longer be recovered for energy (e.g. incineration with heat recovery)",
    "Final disposal with as few pollutants as possible (last option)"
  )
) |>
  kable(align = "cll",
        col.names = c("Rank", "Level", "Meaning"),
        caption = "Waste hierarchy: from prevention (highest priority) to disposal (lowest priority)")


Waste hierarchy: from prevention (highest priority) to disposal (lowest priority)






Rank
Level
Meaning



1
Prevent

2

3

4
Recycling

5
Energy Recovery

6
Disposal

The hierarchy is deliberately to be read as a ranking: the higher up an option is, the more the economic and environmental value of a material is preserved, and the lower the additional resource and energy input required to use it again. Recycling deliberately comes only fourth: in public debate recycling is often equated with sustainability, but from an environmental point of view it is in fact only the third-best available option, because recycling itself also requires energy and processes, and part of the value added originally embodied in the product is lost.
It is precisely this ranking that underlies the concept of the circular economy: instead of disposing of materials after a single use, they are to be kept in the economic cycle for as long as possible at the highest possible level of the hierarchy. For supply chain design, three fundamentally different chain types can be distinguished (Dyckhoff 1998; Chopra and Meindl 2025):

Definition: linear, reverse and circular supply chain
A linear supply chain follows the classic flow of raw material extraction → production → distribution → use → disposal, without materials flowing back into the chain after the use phase.
A reverse supply chain (reverse logistics) supplements this linear flow with a return flow of products, components or packaging from the end customer back to upstream stages – for instance for repair, recycling or proper disposal.
A circular supply chain goes one step further: it is designed from the outset so that returned materials and products are fed back fully into the production and usage cycle, so that primary resources are replaced as completely as possible by secondary resources circulating in the system.

The difference between reverse and circular supply chains is more than semantic: reverse logistics can be motivated purely defensively (legal take-back obligations, warranty processing), whereas a circular supply chain anticipates the return in product and process design and thus makes higher levels of the waste hierarchy – reuse and remanufacturing rather than mere recycling – achievable from the outset.

title: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management
section: 4.7 Design fields of sustainable and circular supply chain management
text:
4.7 Design fields of sustainable and circular supply chain management
To actually implement the circular economy along a supply chain, several design fields must be addressed simultaneously, which can be roughly assigned to three areas:


Circular product design: circularity is already decided during product development – through design decisions that enable later recyclability (e.g. single-material rather than bonded composites), through design for reuse (e.g. modular construction that allows individual components to be replaced instead of the whole product) and through the targeted use of recycled content, i.e. already recovered material as the input for new products.

Sustainable logistics: physical distribution itself is optimised environmentally – through weight reduction of products and packaging (less weight means less energy input per transport), through distance reduction (regional instead of global sourcing and distribution networks) and through transport avoidance in the narrower sense (consolidation of shipments, higher utilisation, substitution of physical by digital processes).

Circular production: production itself is also designed for circularity – through the use of renewable energy, through the use of production waste as input for other processes (industrial symbiosis) and through the recirculation of operating and auxiliary materials (e.g. cooling or process water), which are not disposed of after a single use but reprocessed and reused.

The middle of these three areas – sustainable logistics – directly concerns a decision already familiar to us from earlier chapters: the choice of transport mode. In the following section we work out with our own R calculation how strongly this choice affects the carbon footprint of a shipment.

title: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management
section: 4.8 Sustainable choice of transport mode: a calculation exercise in R
text:
4.8 Sustainable choice of transport mode: a calculation exercise in R
Different modes of transport – truck, rail, inland waterway vessel, ocean vessel, aircraft – differ massively in their carbon efficiency per quantity of goods transported. The customary reference unit for this is the tonne-kilometre (tkm): the carriage of one tonne of cargo over a distance of one kilometre. The CO2 emissions of a specific shipment can then be approximated as
\[
E \;=\; d \cdot m \cdot f
\]
where \(d\) denotes the distance travelled in kilometres, \(m\) the mass transported in tonnes and \(f\) the emission factor of the respective transport mode in grams of CO2 per tonne-kilometre (g CO2/tkm). We work with exactly this formula in the following three R asides, which at the same time introduce three R techniques not yet covered in the previous chapters: importing tabular data with readr, constructing an index with dplyr and building a stacked bar chart with ggplot2::geom_col().

R aside: importing emissions data with readr
So far in this book we have almost always created data directly as a vector or tibble in the R code. In practice, however, data – such as emission factors from an environmental database – are usually available as a text file, typically in CSV format (comma-separated values). The tidyverse package readr provides the function read_csv() for this purpose, which reads a CSV file (or, as here for demonstration purposes, a CSV-formatted text) and automatically detects sensible column types – numbers are imported as double, text as character, without having to specify this by hand.
So that read_csv() interprets a character string as data content rather than as a file path, it is marked with the base R function I() (“as is”):

Code# CO2 emission factors of selected transport modes in g CO2 per tonne-kilometre.
# These are rounded guide values of a realistic order of magnitude
# from the relevant transport and logistics literature, used
# here for illustrative purposes.
emissionsdaten_text <- "Verkehrstraeger,Emissionsfaktor_g_tkm,Kategorie
Truck,62,Road
Rail,22,Rail
Inland vessel,31,Water
Ocean vessel,8,Water
Aircraft,602,Air"

# read_csv() reads the (literal) text and automatically detects
# that the second column is numeric -- I() prevents the
# string from being wrongly interpreted as a file path
emissionsfaktoren <- read_csv(I(emissionsdaten_text), show_col_types = FALSE)

emissionsfaktoren |>
  arrange(Emissionsfaktor_g_tkm) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Transport mode", "g CO₂ / tkm", "Category"),
        align = "lrl",
        caption = "CO2 emission factors of selected transport modes (guide values)")

Even this sorted table reveals the central trade-off of a sustainable choice of transport mode: the ocean vessel has by far the lowest emissions per tonne-kilometre, followed by rail and inland vessel; the truck is considerably higher, and the aircraft causes almost ten times the emissions of a truck per tonne-kilometre. At the same time, it is precisely the lower-emission modes – ship and rail – that are typically slower and less flexible than the truck. This is exactly where the effect of the sustainability dimension on the classic tetrahedron vertices of speed and flexibility, described at the beginning, becomes apparent.


R aside: normalisation and index construction
Absolute emission factors are difficult to assess intuitively (“Is 31 g CO2/tkm a lot or a little?”). In practice, indicators are therefore often normalised, i.e. converted to a common reference value – here to the most economical transport mode available, which receives the index base value of 100. With dplyr::mutate() such an index can be calculated in a single line of code, because min() inside mutate() is automatically computed over the entire column and then applied element-wise to each row:

Code# Emission index: emission factor of each transport mode relative
# to the most economical transport mode (which receives the index value 100) --
# min() is computed once over the whole column and then used in each
# row for the division
emissionsfaktoren <- emissionsfaktoren |>
  mutate(Emissionsindex = round(Emissionsfaktor_g_tkm / min(Emissionsfaktor_g_tkm) * 100, 0))

emissionsfaktoren |>
  arrange(Emissionsindex) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Transport mode", "g CO₂ / tkm", "Category", "Index (ocean vessel = 100)"),
        align = "lrlr",
        caption = "Emission index of transport modes relative to the ocean vessel")

The index is immediately more intuitive than the raw values: according to it, the truck emits almost eight times and the aircraft around 75 times as much CO2 per tonne-kilometre as the ocean vessel. The same normalisation logic – a value is divided by a reference value and multiplied by 100 – is encountered regularly in practice, for instance in price indices, business cycle indicators or indeed sustainability indicators such as CO2 intensity per unit of revenue.

However, the pure emission factors do not yet say anything about a specific shipment, because a real transport chain usually combines several modes of transport. Let us consider a shipment of 20 tonnes of cargo that has to be transported over a total of around 800 kilometres and compare three scenarios: (A) truck transport throughout, (B) rail transport with pre- and on-carriage by truck to and from the terminals, and (C) inland waterway transport, also with pre- and on-carriage by truck.

Codeladung_t <- 20 # tonnes of cargo per shipment, identical in all scenarios

szenarien <- tibble(
  Szenario = c(
    "A: Truck only",
    "B: Rail combined", "B: Rail combined", "B: Rail combined",
    "C: Inland vessel combined", "C: Inland vessel combined", "C: Inland vessel combined"
  ),
  Streckenabschnitt = c(
    "Main carriage",
    "Pre-carriage", "Main carriage", "On-carriage",
    "Pre-carriage", "Main carriage", "On-carriage"
  ),
  Verkehrstraeger = c(
    "Truck",
    "Truck", "Rail", "Truck",
    "Truck", "Inland vessel", "Truck"
  ),
  Distanz_km = c(800, 40, 700, 60, 30, 750, 20)
)

# Add emission factors per transport mode via left_join and
# calculate emissions per route section (g -> kg via /1000)
szenarien <- szenarien |>
  left_join(emissionsfaktoren, by = "Verkehrstraeger") |>
  mutate(Emission_kg = Distanz_km * ladung_t * Emissionsfaktor_g_tkm / 1000)

R aside: a stacked bar chart with geom_col()
To compare the three scenarios not only in a table but also graphically, a stacked bar chart is a good choice: one bar per scenario, whose segments show the emissions of the individual route sections. In ggplot2, geom_col() – unlike geom_bar(), which counts frequencies – creates bars from existing y values; the argument fill = assigns each route section its own fill colour, and ggplot2 automatically stacks the segments on top of each other as soon as several rows share the same x value:

Codeszenarien |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Szenario, y = Emission_kg, fill = Verkehrstraeger)) +
  geom_col(color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Truck"         = cols$atp,
    "Rail"          = cols$top,
    "Inland vessel" = cols$mid
  )) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Emissions (kg CO2)", fill = "Transport mode") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9))



CO2 emissions of three transport scenarios for a 20-tonne shipment over around 800 km



The stacking reveals two things at a glance: first, how much the total height of the bars varies between the scenarios, and second, what share of this total the individual route sections account for – in scenario B, for example, the rail main carriage dominates the emissions, while the truck pre- and on-carriage contribute only small segments.

The calculation impressively confirms what the emission index already suggested: scenario A (truck only) causes around 992 kg CO2, scenario C (inland vessel combined) around 527 kg, and scenario B (rail combined), at around 432 kg CO2, only about 44% of the emissions of scenario A – even though the same quantity is transported over the same total distance in all three scenarios. Combined transport therefore saves a considerable amount of CO2 through the choice of main-carriage mode alone. However, this saving does not come free of charge: transhipment between truck and rail or inland vessel at the terminals costs time and money, transit time increases and flexibility decreases, because rail and ship connections run less frequently and on less flexible schedules than the truck. It is precisely this trade-off between sustainability on the one hand and speed, flexibility and sometimes also cost on the other that we place explicitly once more within the framework of the tetrahedron from Chapter 3 in the last substantive section of this chapter.

title: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management
section: 4.9 Generic strategies of the circular supply chain
text:
4.9 Generic strategies of the circular supply chain
Circular product design cannot be pursued according to the same pattern for every product – a smartphone requires a different circular strategy than packaging. To determine the appropriate generic strategy, a two-dimensional grid of product complexity (low to high) and dynamics of customer preferences (static to dynamic) can be constructed. Combining the two dimensions yields four generic strategies:

Codetibble(
  Quadrant = c(
    "low complexity / dynamic preferences",
    "high complexity / dynamic preferences",
    "low complexity / static preferences",
    "high complexity / static preferences"
  ),
  Normstrategie = c(
    "Design for Recycling",
    "Design for Remanufacture & Reuse",
    "Design for Recycled Content",
    "Design for Repair & Durability"
  ),
  Begründung = c(
    "Short-lived, trend-dependent products are hardly worth remanufacturing; separating materials by type for material recycling is the most efficient circular option.",
    "High material value and high manufacturing complexity justify the more elaborate remanufacturing of entire components or devices, despite changing customer wishes.",
    "Simple, standardised products with stable demand are well suited to using a high proportion of recycled material already in the manufacturing process.",
    "For complex products with long-lasting demand, a design geared to repairability and a long service life pays off particularly well."
  ),
  Beispielprodukte = c(
    "Clothing, furniture",
    "Smartphones, computers",
    "Packaging, steel",
    "Cars, household appliances"
  )
) |>
  kable(align = "llll",
        col.names = c("Quadrant", "Generic strategy", "Rationale", "Example products"),
        caption = "Generic strategies of the circular supply chain by product complexity and preference dynamics") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 12)

The table makes clear that the “circular economy” is not a uniform recipe but sets very different priorities depending on the product category. For packaging and steel – low complexity, stable demand – the focus is on increasing the share of recycled content, because standardised, plannable material loops can be established for this. For smartphones and computers, on the other hand, where both material value and manufacturing complexity are high, remanufacturing – the reprocessing of entire assemblies or devices for resale – pays off, even though customer preferences (new functions, new design) change constantly. Finally, for cars and household appliances, which are complex but in comparatively stable demand, a design geared to repairability from the outset pays off – a principle that links directly to the Renault example from the strategy hierarchy above.

title: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management
section: 4.10 Case study: sustainability at SushiFresh
text:
4.10 Case study: sustainability at SushiFresh

Case study: environmental trade-offs at SushiFresh GmbH
SushiFresh GmbH, introduced in Chapter 3, provides an illustrative example of the sustainability issues faced by a fresh food producer. Three fields of action are at the forefront:


Food waste: Every box left unsold in the evening is not only an economic loss (overage cost \(c^o\) in the newsvendor model, Chapter 8) but also an environmental one: fishing resources, cooling energy and transport effort are destroyed together with the fish. Anyone who puts a monetary value on the environmental impact of unsold goods effectively increases \(c^o\) – the critical ratio falls, and the optimal production quantity decreases. Here, sustainability thus directly shifts an operational decision. According to the waste hierarchy, leftover goods should also be recovered as high up as possible (evening discount before donation before disposal).

Cold chain and transport: The daily, refrigerated delivery in small quantities is emissions-intensive. The location decision (Chapters 5 and 6) influences the kilometres driven; consolidation in a central kitchen reduces inventory and spoilage (Chapter 7) but tends to lengthen the distances. This reveals the trade-off between the concepts of efficiency (consolidation) and decoupling (regional, short distances).

Sourcing of fish: Salmon and tuna are renewable resources, but at risk of overexploitation. The rule of action of balanced use of renewable resources (fishing quotas, certified fisheries) thus becomes a criterion for supplier selection – an example of the cooperation principle with the wholesaler Nord-Fisch (Chapter 9).

In the grid of exposure and environmental orientation, SushiFresh, as a food producer with perishable goods and a critical raw material, is highly exposed. Positioning itself as environmental adaptation – for instance through consistent waste avoidance, certified fish and reusable packaging – also fits the company’s quality and freshness positioning.
crumbs: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management

title: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management
section: 4.11 Trade-offs between sustainability and classic logistics objectives
text:
4.11 Trade-offs between sustainability and classic logistics objectives
This brings us full circle back to the tetrahedron from Chapter 3. The transport mode calculation in the previous section showed by way of example that sustainability objectives can rarely be pursued in isolation, but are almost always in tension with at least one of the four classic vertices of the tetrahedron:


Sustainability versus speed: lower-emission combined transport (rail, inland vessel) is as a rule slower than pure truck transport, because transhipment operations and lower service frequencies cost additional time.

Sustainability versus flexibility/resilience: circular supply chains require functioning reverse logistics, additional capacity for take-back, sorting and reprocessing, and stable partnerships with waste management companies and recyclers – all of which reduces the ability to respond flexibly to changes in demand in the short term.

Sustainability versus cost: recycled materials, renewable energy or more elaborate, repair-friendly designs are often – at least in the short term – more expensive than their conventional alternatives, even if this may be offset in the long term by lower raw material, disposal or regulatory costs.

Sustainability versus quality (in the narrower sense of product performance): recycled content or lightweight construction for weight reduction can – if not carefully designed – lead to trade-offs with the durability or performance of a product.

This observation does not mean that sustainability is fundamentally inferior to the other objectives – rather, it follows exactly the logic we have already encountered for the classic tetrahedron: a trade-off cannot be resolved, only managed through a deliberate, situation-dependent balancing. For the choice of transport mode, this may mean, for instance, reserving the emissions-intensive but fast truck for time-critical legs and using the lower-emission but slower combined transport for plannable main carriages – a solution that is not an extreme point of the tetrahedron but a deliberately chosen profile somewhere in its interior. This is precisely the central message of this chapter and of this book as a whole: supply chain management does not mean maximising a single objective, but designing viable compromises between several, partly conflicting objectives – today explicitly including sustainability.
crumbs: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management

title: 4  Sustainability in Supply Chain Management
section: 4.12 Summary
text:
4.12 Summary
This chapter has introduced sustainability as an independent, cross-cutting dimension of the system of objectives in supply chain management. Starting from the Brundtland definition and the triple bottom line, it became clear that sustainability in the SCM context addresses economic, environmental and social objectives together, without replacing the classic logistics objectives. The grid of environmental exposure and environmental orientation showed that companies can respond very differently to environmental requirements – resistantly, adaptively or offensively – even when their exposure is similar. The four-level hierarchy of rules of action, basic strategies (sufficiency, efficiency, consistency), basic principles and concepts systematised how these responses can be operationalised in concrete terms. Via the waste hierarchy and the distinction between linear, reverse and circular supply chains, we arrived at the circular economy as a central design principle and became acquainted with its three design fields – circular product design, sustainable logistics, circular production – as well as the appropriate generic strategies depending on product complexity and preference dynamics. Finally, our own R calculation on the choice of transport mode quantified by way of example the CO2 savings potential of a more sustainable choice of means of transport – and at the same time showed that this potential does not come free of charge, but follows the same trade-off logic that has accompanied this book throughout, from Chapter 3 up to this point: supply chain management as the management of trade-offs.

Review questions

Explain the Brundtland definition of sustainability and name the three dimensions of the triple bottom line.
To what extent is sustainability a “cross-cutting dimension” of the tetrahedron of trade-offs from Chapter 3, rather than a fifth, equally ranked vertex?
Distinguish the four positions in the grid of environmental exposure and environmental orientation and assign an example company to each.
Describe the four-level hierarchy of environmental SCM strategies and explain the difference between sufficiency, efficiency and consistency using one example each.
Why does recycling only come fourth in the waste hierarchy, even though it is often equated with sustainability in public perception?
How does a circular supply chain differ from a purely reverse supply chain?
Using the R calculation on the choice of transport mode, explain why combined rail transport is not always the “better” choice despite lower emissions.
Which generic strategy of the circular supply chain would you choose for a product with high manufacturing complexity and stable demand that depends little on trends, and why?

title: 5  Facility Location Planning I – Qualitative and Continuous Methods
text:
5.1 Location decisions in strategic supply chain design
Chapter 3 showed that supply chain decisions are guided by a system of objectives that mediates between costs, service level and other target variables, and that logistics costs depend to a considerable extent on the spatial structure of a network. This chapter starts precisely from that spatial structure: the question is where a company should locate its plants, warehouses, transshipment points or sales outlets so that the network as a whole resolves the trade-off between cost and service as well as possible.
Location decisions belong to strategic network planning and differ fundamentally in several respects from operational decisions such as order quantity planning, which is covered in later chapters. First, they are as a rule capital-intensive and binding in the long term: a plant or a central warehouse cannot easily be relocated when demand patterns change. Second, the decision space is multidimensional – besides transport and construction costs, the labour market, infrastructure, taxes, political stability or proximity to customers play a role, and these criteria cannot always be expressed in a common unit (e.g. euros). Third, much of the relevant information is uncertain or has to be assessed subjectively, such as the future development of a regional labour market or “location quality” in the soft sense. These three properties – irreversibility, multidimensionality and uncertainty – explain why facility location planning has developed its own range of methods that goes well beyond a simple cost comparison (Kik 2022).
The facility location planning process typically runs through several phases with a decreasing level of aggregation: at a first, global level, continents or countries are pre-selected on the basis of a few highly aggregated factors (e.g. market access, wage level, political risk). At a second, regional level, the search space is narrowed down to economic areas or regions, where the requirements can already be formulated much more precisely. Only at a third, local level is a concrete site determined – a plot of land, a municipality, a junction in the transport network (Chopra and Meindl 2025).
The slides also highlight why evaluating sites is so difficult: location decisions are irreversible in the short term and create path dependencies (later decisions build on the network once chosen), they are multidimensional (their effects on the system of objectives from Chapter 3 are hard to oversee) and they are subjective (the assessment of soft factors varies between decision-makers, and their importance is weighted differently).
Correspondingly broad is the range of facility location planning methods (Kik 2022). Qualitative methods are heuristic, mostly survey-based methods that bring together an overall picture of opinion and individual assessments. Among the quantitative methods, optimisation requires a clearly delimited decision space (the options) and a one-dimensional system of objectives (e.g. costs); simulation can represent complex, multidimensional cause-and-effect relationships but is laborious and hard to transfer; game-theoretic approaches anticipate the behaviour of competitors, for example to maximise the sales of a retail site; and investment appraisal evaluates sites solely on the basis of monetary quantities over their useful life. This chapter and the next cover qualitative methods and optimisation models, because these two are most frequently combined in practice.
For the actual evaluation of sites (or location regions), two classes of methods are available in principle. Qualitative methods are heuristic, often survey-based evaluation approaches that combine an overall picture from several, usually also soft, criteria; they are particularly suitable for pre-selection among a limited number of discrete alternatives. Quantitative methods, by contrast, formulate the location search as an optimisation problem with an explicit objective function. In this chapter, we cover the scoring model (utility analysis) and the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) from the qualitative family; we then turn to continuous quantitative methods, in which the site is not selected from a given list but determined as an arbitrary point in a plane. The discrete quantitative methods, in which a cost-minimal subset has to be selected from a finite set of potential sites, follow in Chapter 6.
Which location factors are relevant at all depends heavily on the individual case. Roughly, they can be divided into hard factors (transport costs, wages, taxes, land prices – directly measurable in monetary terms) and soft factors (quality of life, image of the region, availability of skilled labour, political stability). Soft factors defy direct cost accounting but influence location quality just as strongly – and qualitative evaluation methods are designed precisely for capturing them systematically.
crumbs: 5  Facility Location Planning I – Qualitative and Continuous Methods

title: 5  Facility Location Planning I – Qualitative and Continuous Methods
text:
Figure 5.1: Phases of location selection from the global to the local level (Chopra and Meindl 2025)



In depth (theory): The Supply Chain Planning Matrix
The lecture places facility location planning within the Supply Chain Planning Matrix (Stadtler 2000). The matrix spans two dimensions: horizontally the value creation processes (procurement, production, distribution, sales), vertically the planning horizon (long, medium and short term). Each cell contains typical planning tasks — such as materials programme and supplier selection (long term, procurement), master production scheduling (medium term, production) or vehicle routing (short term, distribution). The long-term row across all processes is called strategic network planning: it determines which sites exist, what capacity they have and which transport links connect them.
Two properties of this matrix are important for understanding the following chapters. First, decisions act top-down: strategic network planning sets the framework within which medium-term quantity planning and short-term scheduling take place. A poorly located warehouse cannot be compensated for by even the best vehicle routing. Second, there is bottom-up feedback: in order to evaluate sites sensibly, the later operational costs (transport, inventory) must be anticipated at least approximately. Location models therefore work with aggregated quantities — average daily demand, transport cost rates per kilometre — that represent the operational level in simplified form. Chapters 7 to 9 will later show which additional effects (inventory, uncertainty, bullwhip) are not yet visible at this simplified level.










Figure 5.2: Examples of location factors at regional level (Lahner 2020)



5.1.1 The case study of this chapter: SushiFresh GmbH
We apply all methods in this chapter consistently to one and the same continuous case example, which will also accompany us in the following chapters on network and inventory planning: SushiFresh GmbH, a fictitious regional producer of fresh sushi boxes in the Rhine-Main area. SushiFresh supplies six supermarket stores every day with differing but largely known demand:

Code# Six supplied stores with coordinates (WGS84), mean daily demand

6 Offenbach     50.1  8.78    95    22


In addition to the existing deliveries, management is considering building its own production facility in the Rhine-Main area and has identified three commercial plots as candidate sites:

Code# Three candidate sites for the new production facility
standorte <- tibble(
  Standort = c("Wiesbaden-Erbenheim", "Mainz-Hechtsheim", "Raunheim"),
  lat = c(50.0632, 49.9698, 50.0000),
  lon = c(8.2999,  8.2831,  8.4650),
  Fixkosten = c(180000, 210000, 260000)
)
standorte |> rename(Site = Standort, `Fixed costs` = Fixkosten)   # English column names for display

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  Site                  lat   lon `Fixed costs`
  <chr>               <dbl> <dbl>         <dbl>
1 Wiesbaden-Erbenheim  50.1  8.30        180000
2 Mainz-Hechtsheim     50.0  8.28        210000
3 Raunheim             50    8.46        260000

Code# Transport cost rate per box and kilometre (needed again later)
transportkostensatz <- 0.02


Wiesbaden-Erbenheim is a business park with direct access to the A66/A3 and comparatively low land prices; Mainz-Hechtsheim is located on the A60/A63 and close to the Rhine, which favours the delivery of fish, but is more expensive; finally, Raunheim lies close to Frankfurt Airport with very good connections to the A3/A5 but charges the highest commercial rents. The column Fixkosten contains the one-off investment and development costs of the plots (fit-out, refrigeration technology, production equipment); in Chapter 6 they are spread over a useful life of five years and thus converted into annual fixed costs. Together, the six stores demand 845 sushi boxes per day; with 280 boxes, Frankfurt is by far the largest store – we will meet it again in Chapter 8 as an example for the newsvendor formula. This chapter first addresses how SushiFresh can systematically evaluate the three candidate sites and how the company – independently of the three given plots – can determine, purely by calculation, the point in the sales area that minimises transport costs.

title: 5  Facility Location Planning I – Qualitative and Continuous Methods
section: 5.2 Qualitative location evaluation
text:
5.2 Qualitative location evaluation

5.2.1 The scoring model (utility analysis)

Definition: Scoring model (utility analysis)
The scoring model (utility analysis, German Nutzwertanalyse, NWA) is an additive multi-criteria evaluation method. For each alternative \(j\), an overall utility value \(N_j\) is formed across all criteria \(k=1,\dots,K\) as the weighted sum of the partial utility values \(w_{jk}\): \[
N_j = \sum_{k=1}^{K} g_k \cdot w_{jk}, \qquad \sum_{k=1}^{K} g_k = 1,
\] where \(g_k\) is the weight of criterion \(k\) and \(w_{jk}\) is the rating of alternative \(j\) with respect to criterion \(k\) (usually awarded on a points scale, e.g. 0–10).

The scoring model follows a clearly structured, five-step procedure: first, the relevant evaluation criteria are defined, then their weights are determined (e.g. by expert estimation or pairwise comparison). Next, the alternatives are rated for each criterion, the weighted partial utility values are aggregated into the overall utility value, and finally the alternatives are ranked according to this overall utility value.
This additive structure makes the scoring model simple to apply and easy to follow – but it also harbours a methodological weakness that is best illustrated with a numerical example.






NoteCase example: Production site for SushiFresh



SushiFresh management evaluates the three candidate sites Wiesbaden-Erbenheim, Mainz-Hechtsheim and Raunheim on the basis of three criteria – weighted equally here for simplicity: transport proximity to the six stores, rental costs and availability of skilled labour. Wiesbaden-Erbenheim is strongest on rental costs (lowest fixed costs), Raunheim on transport proximity to the store network, while Mainz-Hechtsheim leads on the availability of skilled labour – it offers good access to training institutions in catering and food technology.



Code# Raw data of the case study: three criteria, equally weighted (1/3 per criterion),
# ratings of the three candidate sites on a scale from 0 (poor) to 10 (good)
nwa <- tibble(
  Kriterium = c(
    "Transport proximity",
    "Rental costs",
    "Skilled labour availability"
  ),
  Gewicht = c(1/3, 1/3, 1/3),
  `WI-Erbenheim`  = c(5, 8, 2),
  `MZ-Hechtsheim` = c(2, 5, 8),
  Raunheim        = c(8, 2, 5)
)

# Overall utility value per site: sum of weight * rating across all criteria
nutzwert <- c(
  `WI-Erbenheim`  = sum(nwa$Gewicht * nwa$`WI-Erbenheim`),
  `MZ-Hechtsheim` = sum(nwa$Gewicht * nwa$`MZ-Hechtsheim`),
  Raunheim        = sum(nwa$Gewicht * nwa$Raunheim)
)
nutzwert

            5             5             5

At first glance, the result is surprising: all three sites achieve exactly the same overall utility value of 5.0 – even though their strength–weakness profiles are completely different: Wiesbaden-Erbenheim scores on rental costs but loses on the availability of skilled labour; Mainz-Hechtsheim scores on skilled labour but loses on transport proximity; Raunheim scores on transport proximity but loses on rental costs. The reason for the identical result lies in the additive aggregation: a weak rating on one criterion can be compensated by a correspondingly strong rating on another criterion. This compensability is the central methodological weakness of the scoring model. It raises several follow-on problems:

The additive model can only be interpreted to a limited extent, because it implicitly assumes that the criteria are utility-independent – i.e. that the utility contribution of one criterion does not change depending on how well or badly other criteria turn out. In practice, this assumption is often questionable.
The results are sensitive to the chosen weighting; small shifts in the weights \(g_k\) can reverse the ranking of the alternatives.
There is a risk of objective splitting: an objective that is actually coherent is broken down into many individual criteria whose weights can hardly be set in a comprehensible way.

These weaknesses motivate a method that derives the criteria and alternative weights more systematically – via pairwise comparisons instead of directly estimated scores: the Analytic Hierarchy Process.

5.2.2 The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP)

Definition: Analytic Hierarchy Process
The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) is a multi-level multi-criteria decision method that derives priorities – for criteria as well as for alternatives – from pairwise comparisons. Instead of estimating scores directly, the decision-maker assesses two elements against each other at a time (“How much more important is A than B?”) on a defined scale. From the resulting pairwise comparison matrix, a priority vector is then derived that can be interpreted as a ranking or weighting.

The AHP proceeds in five steps: (1) form pairwise comparisons between all alternatives for each evaluation criterion, (2) derive a ranking of the alternatives for each criterion from these (“synthesis”), (3) form pairwise comparisons between all evaluation criteria, (4) derive a ranking of the criteria from these, and (5) combine both rankings into an overall score per alternative.
The steps follow a bottom-up hierarchy (Figure 5.3): first, the contribution of each alternative to each criterion is assessed; then the contribution of each criterion to the overall objective; finally, both are combined to identify the best alternative.




Bottom level: Determine how the alternatives contribute to the criteria.


⇓


Medium level: Determine how the evaluation criteria contribute to achieving the objective.


⇓


Top level: Determine the best of the given alternatives (objective).




Figure 5.3: Bottom-up hierarchy of the AHP (after Klein and Scholl 2011, 361)


Pairwise comparisons are usually recorded on a nine-point scale ranging from “equally important” (value 1) to “extremely preferred” (value 9); the reciprocal values \(1/9\) to \(1\) express the opposite direction of preference. A pairwise comparison matrix \(A\) with entries \(a_{ij}\) (“how much more important is \(i\) than \(j\)?”) is therefore reciprocal: \(a_{ji} = 1/a_{ij}\), and the diagonal always contains ones. From a perfectly consistent matrix, the priority vector could be read directly from a single row or column; in practice, however, expert assessments are never perfectly consistent, which is why the priority vector is determined by averaging – computationally via the dominant eigenvector of the matrix, approximated e.g. by the geometric mean of the rows.






NoteCase example: AHP for the SushiFresh production site



Instead of estimating scores directly, SushiFresh management now compares the three candidate sites Wiesbaden-Erbenheim, Mainz-Hechtsheim and Raunheim pairwise – both against each other for each criterion and the three criteria transport proximity, rental costs and availability of skilled labour against one another.


To represent the three pairwise comparison matrices (one per criterion) and the criteria comparison matrix in R, we need a data structure that – unlike a data.frame – is rectangular and purely numeric from the outset and can be processed using the rules of linear algebra (matrix multiplication, transposition): the matrix.

R aside: Matrices in R
A matrix is created with matrix(). The vector of values is arranged row-wise or column-wise into the desired shape; byrow = TRUE ensures that the values are filled in row by row (instead of R’s default column-wise order). Row and column names can be assigned with dimnames. Individual elements, entire rows or columns are accessed via square brackets with two indices [row, column] – an empty index stands for “all”:

Code# Create a 3x3 matrix with row and column names: pairwise comparison
# of the three candidate sites with respect to the criterion transport proximity
m <- matrix(
  c(1,   2,   1/2,
    1/2, 1,   1/3,
    2,   3,   1),
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c("WI-Erb", "MZ-Hech", "Raunheim"), c("WI-Erb", "MZ-Hech", "Raunheim"))
)
m

         WI-Erb MZ-Hech  Raunheim
WI-Erb      1.0       2 0.5000000
MZ-Hech     0.5       1 0.3333333
Raunheim    2.0       3 1.0000000

Code# Single element: row 1, column 2 -> "How strongly is WI-Erb preferred over MZ-Hech?"
m[1, 2]

[1] 2

Code# Entire 2nd row: comparison of MZ-Hech with all three sites
m[2, ]

   WI-Erb   MZ-Hech  Raunheim 
0.5000000 1.0000000 0.3333333 

Code# Dimensions of the matrix (rows, columns)
dim(m)

[1] 3 3


For two matrices X (dimension \(m \times n\)) and Y (dimension \(n \times p\)), the operator %*% computes the matrix product \(X\,Y\) (dimension \(m \times p\)) in the sense of linear algebra – unlike X * Y, which only multiplies element-wise. We use %*% twice below: once to combine a distance matrix with a demand vector, and once to combine the criteria weights with the ratings of the alternatives into an overall AHP score.

This allows the three pairwise comparison matrices from the case example to be reproduced directly in R:

Code# Pairwise comparisons of the three candidate sites per criterion (Saaty scale 1-9 or reciprocals)
transportnaehe <- matrix(
  c(1,   2,   1/2,
    1/2, 1,   1/3,
    2,   3,   1),
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c("WI-Erb", "MZ-Hech", "Raunheim"), c("WI-Erb", "MZ-Hech", "Raunheim"))
)

mietkosten <- matrix(
  c(1,   2,   4,
    1/2, 1,   2,
    1/4, 1/2, 1),
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c("WI-Erb", "MZ-Hech", "Raunheim"), c("WI-Erb", "MZ-Hech", "Raunheim"))
)

fachkraefte <- matrix(
  c(1,   1/7, 2,
    7,   1,   5,
    1/2, 1/5, 1),
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c("WI-Erb", "MZ-Hech", "Raunheim"), c("WI-Erb", "MZ-Hech", "Raunheim"))
)


The matrix mietkosten (rental costs) directly reflects the fixed costs of the three plots (€180,000 / €210,000 / €260,000): Wiesbaden-Erbenheim is clearly preferred over Raunheim with a value of 4. For each of these three matrices, ahp_priority_vector() from R/scm_functions.R returns the corresponding priority vector (the relative site preferences per criterion). Instead of calling the function three times individually, we bundle the three matrices in a list and apply the function to each list element with sapply().

R aside: sapply() and apply()
sapply(X, FUN) applies a function FUN to each element of X and simplifies the result to a vector or matrix where possible. If X – as here – is a list of matrices and FUN returns a vector of the same length for each element, the result is a matrix in which each column corresponds to one list element. sapply() thus saves writing a loop by hand when the same function is to be applied repeatedly to several objects.
Closely related is apply(X, MARGIN, FUN), which applies a function row-wise (MARGIN = 1) or column-wise (MARGIN = 2) to a single matrix. Internally, ahp_priority_vector() uses exactly this pattern to compute the geometric mean for each row of a pairwise comparison matrix – a common, numerically stable approximation of the actually exact eigenvector method.

Code# List of all three criteria matrices
kriterien_matrizen <- list(
  Transport      = transportnaehe,
  Rent           = mietkosten,
  Skilled_labour = fachkraefte
)

# sapply() applies ahp_priority_vector() to each matrix in the list and
# returns the three preference vectors as a joint matrix (sites x criteria)
praeferenz_matrix <- sapply(kriterien_matrizen, ahp_priority_vector)
praeferenz_matrix

         Transport      Rent Skilled_labour
WI-Erb   0.2969613 0.5714286      0.1498987
MZ-Hech  0.1634241 0.2857143      0.7444632
Raunheim 0.5396146 0.1428571      0.1056381



The table praeferenz_matrix shows: Raunheim clearly dominates on transport proximity (approx. 54%), Wiesbaden-Erbenheim on rental costs (approx. 57%), and Mainz-Hechtsheim very clearly on the availability of skilled labour (approx. 74%) – so, as in the scoring model, each of the three sites plays to a different strength. This completes step 2 of the AHP (synthesis per criterion); what is still missing is the ranking of the three criteria themselves (steps 3 and 4), which again requires a pairwise comparison matrix – this time between the criteria rather than between the sites.

Code# Pairwise comparison of the three evaluation criteria with one another
kriterien_vergleich <- matrix(
  c(1,   3,   2,
    1/3, 1,   1/5,
    1/2, 5,   1),
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(
    c("Transport", "Rent", "Skilled_labour"),
    c("Transport", "Rent", "Skilled_labour")
  )
)

kriterien_gewichte <- ahp_priority_vector(kriterien_vergleich)
kriterien_gewichte

     Transport           Rent Skilled_labour 
     0.5076026      0.1132686      0.3791288 


With around 51%, transport proximity receives by far the highest weight, followed by availability of skilled labour (approx. 38%); with around 11%, rental costs play a comparatively minor role. Before we use these weights further, we check whether the underlying pairwise comparison matrix is consistent enough at all to allow robust conclusions. Consistency here means transitivity of intensities: anyone who considers transport proximity three times as important as rental costs (\(a_{TM}=3\)) and skilled labour five times as important as rental costs (\(a_{FM}=5\)) should logically consider transport proximity only \(3/5 = 0.6\) times as important as skilled labour. In fact, however, \(a_{TF}=2\) was stated – i.e. transport proximity twice as important as skilled labour. A perfectly consistent matrix satisfies \(a_{ik} = a_{ij}\cdot a_{jk}\) for all \(i,j,k\); the more strongly this condition is violated, the larger the largest eigenvalue of the matrix becomes relative to \(n\). Formally, the consistency index \[
CI = \frac{\bar{\lambda} - n}{n - 1}
\] is computed for this purpose, where \(n\) is the number of criteria and \(\bar{\lambda}\) is the (approximated) largest eigenvalue of the matrix, obtained by dividing the product of the matrix and the priority vector component-wise by the priority vector and taking the average. Relative to a randomly generated random index \(RI\) (tabulated by Saaty as a function of \(n\)), this yields the consistency ratio \[
CR = \frac{CI}{RI}.
\] As a rule of thumb, a matrix is considered sufficiently consistent if \(CR < 0.10\); for larger values, the pairwise comparisons should be revised.

Codekonsistenz <- ahp_consistency(kriterien_vergleich, kriterien_gewichte)
konsistenz

$lambda_max
[1] 3.163235

$CI
[1] 0.08161727

$CR
[1] 0.1407194

$consistent
[1] FALSE


With \(CI \approx 0.082\) and \(CR \approx 0.14\), the criteria matrix lies above the 10% threshold. The intransitivity between transport proximity, skilled labour and rental costs described above is therefore too large for the weights to be adopted unchecked. In practice, one would ask the decision-makers to reconsider their comparisons – for instance, correcting the comparison of transport proximity versus skilled labour from 2 to 1/2, which would make the matrix almost consistent. For the teaching example, we continue calculating with the original judgements from the lecture but keep this caveat in mind: it shows precisely the benefit of the AHP, which – unlike the scoring model – makes inconsistencies visible in the first place.






NoteNote on the lecture slides



On the slides, the consistency value \(CI = (\bar{P}-n)/(n-1) \approx 0.08\) is calculated. This value is the consistency index \(CI\). For the verdict “consistent/inconsistent”, it still has to be divided by the random index \(RI = 0.58\) (for \(n=3\)); only the resulting consistency ratio \(CR \approx 0.14\) is compared with the 10% threshold.


In the last step, the site–criteria matrix and the criteria weight vector are combined into an overall score per site using the matrix product %*% – exactly the operation announced in the R aside on matrices:

Codescores <- praeferenz_matrix %*% kriterien_gewichte
scores

              [,1]
WI-Erb   0.2722942
MZ-Hech  0.3975644
Raunheim 0.3301414


Mainz-Hechtsheim achieves the highest value with a score of around 0.398, ahead of Raunheim (0.330) and Wiesbaden-Erbenheim (0.272). At first glance, the result is surprising, since by far the highest criterion weight belongs to transport proximity, where Raunheim clearly leads. The decisive factor is the strength of the preference on skilled labour: there, Mainz-Hechtsheim is rated as “strongly preferred” (7) over Wiesbaden-Erbenheim and receives around 74% of the criterion weight – with a criterion weight for skilled labour of around 38%, this is enough to more than make up for the deficit on transport proximity. The lead over Raunheim is narrow, however, and in view of the inconsistency found in the criteria matrix, a sensitivity analysis of the weights (see review questions) would be advisable before a final recommendation.
Compared with the scoring model, the AHP has two major advantages: first, pairwise comparison increases transparency, because decision-makers only have to weigh two elements against each other at a time instead of a complete ranking. Second, the AHP offers less scope for bias in individual assessments than the scoring model, because irrational or contradictory judgements can be explicitly uncovered via the consistency index – a diagnostic tool that the scoring model lacks and that actually triggers in the case example. Whether the qualitative recommendation in favour of Mainz-Hechtsheim is also confirmed by a purely quantitative cost analysis is deliberately left open at this point – we will return to it at the end of this chapter and then again in detail in Chapter 6.

In depth (theory): Why the eigenvector? – Computational approaches of the AHP
The idea of the AHP (Saaty 1980) is best understood starting from the ideal case. Suppose the “true” weights of the alternatives are \(w_1,\dots,w_n\) and the decision-maker judges without error. Then, as pairwise comparisons, they would state exactly the ratios \(a_{ij} = w_i/w_j\). Multiplying such a matrix by the weight vector gives \[
(A\,w)_i = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{w_i}{w_j}\, w_j = n\, w_i \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad A\,w = n\,w .
\] The weight vector is therefore an eigenvector of the pairwise comparison matrix for the eigenvalue \(n\). Because the matrix has rank 1 in this ideal case, all other eigenvalues are zero, and \(n\) is the largest eigenvalue \(\lambda_{\max}\). Real judgements are not perfectly consistent; then \(\lambda_{\max} > n\), and Saaty proposes using the eigenvector belonging to the largest eigenvalue as the “best possible” weight vector. The deviation \(\lambda_{\max} - n\) at the same time measures how strongly the judgements deviate from the consistent ideal case – from this, the consistency index \(CI = (\lambda_{\max}-n)/(n-1)\) is derived. The random index \(RI\) is the average \(CI\) value of randomly filled reciprocal matrices of the same size; the consistency ratio \(CR = CI/RI\) thus compares the observed inconsistency with that of a decision-maker “rolling dice”.
In practice, the eigenvector is often approximated. Two methods are common:


Column normalisation and row mean (the approach on the lecture slides): each column is divided by its column sum, and the average is then taken across each row. In the consistent case, each normalised column is already exactly the weight vector; in the case of inconsistency, averaging evens out the deviations.

Geometric row mean (used in ahp_priority_vector()): for each row, \(\left(\prod_j a_{ij}\right)^{1/n}\) is formed and then normalised. This method also yields exactly \(w\) in the consistent case and is moreover invariant to transposition (taking reciprocals) of the judgements.

For nearly consistent matrices, both methods and the exact eigenvector yield practically identical values; with stronger inconsistencies, they differ in the third decimal place. The following code reproduces the approach on the slides for the criteria matrix and compares it with the geometric mean and the exact eigenvector returned by eigen():

Code# 1) Column normalisation and row mean (approach on the slides)
spalten_normiert <- sweep(kriterien_vergleich, 2, colSums(kriterien_vergleich), "/")
w_spalten <- rowMeans(spalten_normiert)

# 2) Geometric row mean (ahp_priority_vector)
w_geo <- ahp_priority_vector(kriterien_vergleich)

# 3) Exact eigenvector for the largest eigenvalue
ev    <- eigen(kriterien_vergleich)
w_eig <- Re(ev$vectors[, 1]) / sum(Re(ev$vectors[, 1]))

round(cbind(`Column normalisation` = w_spalten, `Geometric mean` = w_geo, Eigenvector = w_eig), 3)

               Column normalisation Geometric mean Eigenvector
Transport                     0.501          0.508       0.508
Rent                          0.118          0.113       0.113
Skilled_labour                0.380          0.379       0.379

CodeRe(ev$values[1])   # largest eigenvalue lambda_max (> n = 3 due to inconsistency)

[1] 3.163235
