title: 5  Facility Location Planning I – Qualitative and Continuous Methods
section: 5.3 Continuous facility location planning: the Steiner–Weber model
text:
5.3 Continuous facility location planning: the Steiner–Weber model
Both the scoring model and the AHP presuppose that a manageable set of discrete alternatives is already available to choose from – at SushiFresh, the three commercial plots actually available. Often, however, the location question arises differently: what is sought is not the best of several given addresses, but the point in the plane that minimises transport costs to a set of customer locations – at SushiFresh, the point in the Rhine-Main area that minimises the total distance to the six stores, regardless of whether a plot is available there at all. This question is addressed by continuous facility location planning, whose classic model goes back to Alfred Weber and is usually referred to in the literature as the Steiner–Weber model (Cooper 1968; Thonemann 2023).
The model makes four simplifying assumptions: there is a homogeneous plane (the sales area) containing a finite number of customer locations; for each customer location, a demand quantity is given that must be served in full; transport costs depend linearly on distance and quantity transported; and the time dimension is disregarded. Under these assumptions, the objective function is \[
\min_{(x,y)}\; Z(x,y) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \cdot d\big((x,y),(u_i,v_i)\big),
\] where \((x,y)\) are the sought coordinates of the new site, \((u_i, v_i)\) the coordinates of customer location \(i\), \(a_i\) its demand (at SushiFresh: boxes per day) and \(d(\cdot)\) a distance measure still to be chosen.
The choice of \(d(\cdot)\) is by no means secondary; it determines both the computational method and the result. For sites within a country or region in which transport routes run approximately “as the crow flies”, the Euclidean distance is suitable: \[
d^{\text{eukl}}\big((x,y),(u_i,v_i)\big) = \sqrt{(x-u_i)^2 + (y-v_i)^2}.
\] In city centres with a rectangular street grid or for in-plant transport along orthogonal aisles, the Manhattan distance (also rectilinear or \(L_1\) distance) is often more realistic: \[
d^{\text{man}}\big((x,y),(u_i,v_i)\big) = |x-u_i| + |y-v_i|.
\] For actual network planning, in turn, road distances – the shortest paths in a real transport network – are the most accurate, but also the most laborious to compute, as they require a digital road network and a routing service. The following code shows by way of example how these three distance measures between the candidate site Wiesbaden-Erbenheim and the Frankfurt store can be computed with the packages sf, osrm and leaflet and compared on an interactive map. Since the road distance requires an online routing service (OSRM) and the retrieval of map tiles, the chunk is marked eval: false and is not executed during rendering.

Code# Note: this chunk requires internet access (OpenStreetMap map tiles
# and the OSRM routing service for the road distance) and is therefore not
# executed when rendering the book (eval: false) - it only serves to
# illustrate how the three distance measures are compared in practice.

library(sf)
library(osrm)
library(leaflet)

standort_wi <- st_as_sf(data.frame(id = "Wiesbaden-Erbenheim", lon = 8.2999, lat = 50.0632),
                         coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
filiale_ffm <- st_as_sf(data.frame(id = "Frankfurt", lon = 8.6821, lat = 50.1109),
                         coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

# Shortest path in the real road network via the OSRM service
route <- osrmRoute(src = standort_wi, dst = filiale_ffm)

# Interactive map: road route in red, site/store as markers
leaflet() |>
  addProviderTiles(providers$OpenStreetMap.Mapnik) |>
  addPolylines(data = route, color = "red") |>
  addCircleMarkers(data = standort_wi, color = "black") |>
  addCircleMarkers(data = filiale_ffm, color = "purple")


In practice, the road distance between two points is almost always greater than the Euclidean and usually also greater than the Manhattan distance, since real road networks are neither straight nor strictly orthogonal. For the following derivations, we restrict ourselves – as the literature on the Steiner–Weber model predominantly does – to Euclidean and Manhattan distances, because closed-form or efficient iterative solution methods can be given for both (Daskin 2013; Drezner and Hamacher 2002).
For the numerical examples in this section, we consistently use the SushiFresh data set with the six stores introduced above. Since the centre of gravity and the Weiszfeld algorithm were originally derived for planar (Cartesian) coordinates, we initially treat longitude and latitude here approximately as planar \(x\)/\(y\) coordinates ($x = $ longitude, $y = $ latitude) – a deliberate didactic simplification whose limits we make explicitly visible at the end of this section using the haversine formula.

Code# Bubble chart: position = store, bubble size = demand
ggplot(filialen, aes(x = lon, y = lat)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = mu), color = "#c97a2b", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Filiale), vjust = -1.2, size = 3.2) +
  labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", size = "Demand a (boxes/day)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








5.3.1 Centre of gravity: the quadratic approximation
The simplest approach to the Steiner–Weber problem is obtained if, in the objective function, one minimises not the (non-differentiable) Euclidean distance itself but its square: \[
\min_{(x,y)}\; \tilde{Z}(x,y) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \left[(x-u_i)^2 + (y-v_i)^2\right].
\] This objective function is separable in \(x\) and \(y\) and differentiable everywhere, so the minimum can be determined directly via the necessary optimality conditions. The partial derivative with respect to \(x\) is \[
\frac{\partial \tilde{Z}}{\partial x} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} 2\,a_i\,(x - u_i) \stackrel{!}{=} 0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i\, u_i,
\] and analogously for \(y\). Solving for \(x\) and \(y\) yields the centre of gravity (CoG):

Definition: Centre of gravity \[
x^{CoG} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i\, u_i}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i},
\qquad
y^{CoG} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i\, v_i}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i}.
\] The centre of gravity is the demand-weighted centroid of all customer locations and minimises the sum of the weighted squared Euclidean distances.

Since this derivation essentially consists of only three computational steps – calculating total demand, forming weighted coordinate sums, dividing – it can be reproduced in R directly and without any aids:

Code# Step 1: sum up total demand across all stores
gesamtnachfrage <- sum(filialen$mu)

# Step 2: form the demand-weighted sum of longitude and latitude
gewichtete_summe_lon <- sum(filialen$mu * filialen$lon)
gewichtete_summe_lat <- sum(filialen$mu * filialen$lat)

# Step 3: dividing by total demand yields the centroid
cog_lon <- gewichtete_summe_lon / gesamtnachfrage
cog_lat <- gewichtete_summe_lat / gesamtnachfrage

c(lon = cog_lon, lat = cog_lat)

      lon       lat 
 8.524064 50.041020 


As a check, the ready-made function center_of_gravity() from R/scm_functions.R – which encapsulates the same calculation but expects a data.frame with columns x, y, demand – returns the same result:

Codecenter_of_gravity(data.frame(x = filialen$lon, y = filialen$lat, demand = filialen$mu))

        x         y 
 8.524064 50.041020 


The centre of gravity lies at \((x^{CoG}, y^{CoG}) \approx (8.5241; 50.0410)\) – geographically roughly between Frankfurt and Rüsselsheim, well to the east of the three candidate sites. It is attractive because it can be computed in closed form without iteration. Strictly speaking, however, it does not solve the original Steiner–Weber problem, only its squared variant – and the two optima need not be identical. In particular, the CoG is more sensitive to distant outlier customers, because squared distances weight large distances disproportionately. For the actual, non-squared objective function, a different method is needed.

5.3.2 The Weiszfeld algorithm: iterative solution of the true problem
To solve the original problem with linear (non-squared) Euclidean distances, we again form the necessary optimality condition, this time for \[
Z(x,y) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \sqrt{(x-u_i)^2+(y-v_i)^2}.
\] The partial derivative with respect to \(x\) is \[
\frac{\partial Z}{\partial x} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i\, \frac{x - u_i}{d_i(x,y)} \stackrel{!}{=} 0,
\qquad d_i(x,y) = \sqrt{(x-u_i)^2+(y-v_i)^2}.
\] Unlike with the squared objective function, \(x\) here also appears in the denominator (via \(d_i\)), so the equation cannot be solved directly for \(x\). The way out is to treat the \(d_i\) in a given iteration step as known (namely from the previous iteration) and then solve the equation for \(x\). With the abbreviation \[
g_i(x,y) = \frac{a_i}{d_i(x,y)}
\] this yields the update rule of the Weiszfeld algorithm: \[
x_{t+1} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n u_i\, g_i(x_t,y_t)}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x_t,y_t)},
\qquad
y_{t+1} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n v_i\, g_i(x_t,y_t)}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x_t,y_t)}.
\] It is remarkable that this update rule formally looks like a centre-of-gravity update – except that the iteration-dependent weights \(g_i(x_t,y_t)\) are used instead of the fixed demand weights \(a_i\). Customers who are close to the current site and have high demand receive a high weight \(g_i\) and pull the next site more strongly in their direction. It makes sense to start with the centre of gravity as the initial solution \((x_0,y_0)\) and to repeat the update rule until the position hardly changes from one iteration to the next.
To programme this iterative procedure in R, we need a control structure that repeats a block of calculations several times: the loop.

R aside: for and while loops
A for loop repeats a code block for each element of a vector – it is suitable when the number of iterations is known in advance (e.g. “once per candidate site”):

Code# for loop: fixed pass over a known number of values -
# here over the three candidate sites
for (i in seq_len(nrow(standorte))) {
  cat("Site:", standorte$Standort[i],
      "- Fixed costs:", standorte$Fixkosten[i], "EUR/year\n")
}

Site: Wiesbaden-Erbenheim - Fixed costs: 180000 EUR/year
Site: Mainz-Hechtsheim - Fixed costs: 210000 EUR/year
Site: Raunheim - Fixed costs: 260000 EUR/year

Code# while loop: repetition as long as a condition is met -
# the number of iterations is not fixed in advance
schritt <- 1
wert <- 100
while (wert > 1) {
  wert <- wert / 2      # halve the value in each step
  schritt <- schritt + 1
}
cat("After", schritt, "steps the value is below 1:", round(wert, 4), "\n")

After 8 steps the value is below 1: 0.7812 


A while loop checks a logical condition before each pass and repeats the code block as long as it is TRUE – it is therefore a better fit when it is not known in advance how many steps are needed, only when to stop. This is exactly the situation with the Weiszfeld algorithm: we do not know in advance after how many iterations the solution will have converged sufficiently. In practice, both principles are therefore usually combined: a for loop with a fixed upper limit on iterations as a safety net, combined with an if exit (break or return) as soon as the actual convergence criterion is met. The following R aside shows how such a pattern can be wrapped in a custom function.


R aside: a function with several parameters and control flow
So far in this book, we have mainly written functions with one or two arguments. Iterative methods such as Weiszfeld, by contrast, typically require several parameters: the input data, an optional starting value, a tolerance threshold for the stopping criterion and a maximum number of iterations as a safety net in case the tolerance is never reached. Such optional parameters are given a default value in the function definition (e.g. tol = 1e-6), which is only overridden if a different value is explicitly passed when calling the function.

Codeweiszfeld_manual <- function(daten, x0 = NULL, y0 = NULL,
                              tol = 1e-6, max_iter = 100) {
  # daten:    data.frame with columns u, v (coordinates) and a (demand)
  # x0, y0:   starting coordinates; if NULL, the centre of gravity is used
  # tol:      tolerance threshold for the stopping criterion (convergence)
  # max_iter: maximum number of iterations as a safety net

  # If not specified: use the centre of gravity as the initial solution
  if (is.null(x0)) x0 <- sum(daten$a * daten$u) / sum(daten$a)
  if (is.null(y0)) y0 <- sum(daten$a * daten$v) / sum(daten$a)

  x <- x0
  y <- y0

  # for loop with fixed upper limit max_iter as a safety net
  for (t in 1:max_iter) {

    # distance from the current site (x,y) to each store
    d <- sqrt((x - daten$u)^2 + (y - daten$v)^2)

    # avoid division by 0 if the site lies exactly on a store
    d[d < 1e-10] <- 1e-10

    # iteration weights g_i = a_i / d_i according to the Weiszfeld update rule
    g <- daten$a / d

    # updated coordinates as weighted mean with weights g_i
    x_neu <- sum(daten$u * g) / sum(g)
    y_neu <- sum(daten$v * g) / sum(g)

    # distance moved between two successive iterations
    delta <- sqrt((x_neu - x)^2 + (y_neu - y)^2)

    x <- x_neu
    y <- y_neu

    # control flow: stop as soon as the change is sufficiently small
    if (delta < tol) {
      return(list(x = x, y = y, iterations = t, converged = TRUE))
    }
  }

  # In case the loop ran through without convergence
  list(x = x, y = y, iterations = max_iter, converged = FALSE)
}


The if block inside the loop is the actual control flow: after each iteration step, it checks whether the stopping criterion is met and, if so, terminates the function early via return() – otherwise the loop continues until either convergence occurs or max_iter is reached.

Let us apply weiszfeld_manual() to the SushiFresh store data set (passing longitude as u, latitude as v and demand as a):

Codeergebnis <- weiszfeld_manual(
  data.frame(u = filialen$lon, v = filialen$lat, a = filialen$mu),
  tol = 1e-6, max_iter = 100
)
ergebnis

The algorithm converges after 69 iterations to the site \((x,y) \approx (8.6135; 50.0676)\) – considerably closer to Frankfurt than the centre of gravity. As a check, the ready-made function weiszfeld() from R/scm_functions.R (which implements the same algorithm internally but additionally logs the course of all iterations) returns an identical result:

Codeweiszfeld_check <- weiszfeld(data.frame(x = filialen$lon, y = filialen$lat, demand = filialen$mu))
c(x = weiszfeld_check$x, y = weiszfeld_check$y,
  iterations = weiszfeld_check$iterations, converged = weiszfeld_check$converged)

         x          y iterations  converged 
  8.613533  50.067561  69.000000   1.000000 


This confirms the theoretical expectation: the CoG is a solution that can be computed quickly but is only approximate; the iterative Weiszfeld algorithm solves the actual Steiner–Weber problem and, compared with the CoG, noticeably shifts the site towards Frankfurt – by far the store with the highest demand (280 of 845 boxes/day). How strongly this actually affects the real (geographic) distance to each individual store is examined in the next section using the haversine formula.
The lecture shows how the algorithm approaches the optimum using a deliberately distant starting point \((x_0, y_0) = (8.75;\ 49.85)\) south-east of Darmstadt. To trace the path, this time we log every iteration:

Codedaten_w <- data.frame(u = filialen$lon, v = filialen$lat, a = filialen$mu)
x <- 8.75; y <- 49.85                      # distant starting point as in the lecture
verlauf <- tibble(t = 0, x = x, y = y)

for (t in 1:15) {
  d <- sqrt((x - daten_w$u)^2 + (y - daten_w$v)^2)
  g <- daten_w$a / d                        # iteration weights
  x <- sum(daten_w$u * g) / sum(g)
  y <- sum(daten_w$v * g) / sum(g)
  verlauf <- add_row(verlauf, t = t, x = x, y = y)
}

The very first step already bridges most of the distance; after that, the steps quickly become smaller. The last decimal places, however, stabilise only slowly: before the tolerance of \(10^{-6}\) is reached, the algorithm needs several dozen iterations (see above). This is typical of the Weiszfeld algorithm when the optimum lies close to a high-demand customer – here Frankfurt – because its iteration weight \(g_i = a_i/d_i\) grows strongly as the distance decreases and the steps become ever shorter.

In depth (theory): Why does the Weiszfeld algorithm converge?
As a sum of weighted Euclidean norms, the objective function \(Z(x,y) = \sum_i a_i\, d_i(x,y)\) is convex: each individual distance function \(d_i\) is a “cone” with its apex at the customer location, and a non-negatively weighted sum of convex functions is again convex. It follows that every local minimum is also a global minimum — there are no “traps” in which a method could get stuck. If the customer locations do not all lie on a straight line, \(Z\) is even strictly convex and the optimum is unique.
The algorithm goes back to Weiszfeld (1937). It can be shown that each iteration step does not increase the objective function value: in each step, the update rule minimises a quadratic auxiliary function that touches \(Z\) at the current point and lies above \(Z\) everywhere (majorisation principle). The minimum of the auxiliary function is precisely the weighted mean with the weights \(g_i = a_i/d_i\) — i.e. the update rule. Since the objective function value decreases monotonically and is bounded below, the method converges. Special treatment is only necessary if an iteration falls exactly on a customer location (\(d_i = 0\), division by zero); in practice, this case is caught, as in weiszfeld_manual(), by a small lower bound for \(d_i\).
The economic interpretation of the optimality condition \(\sum_i a_i (x-u_i)/d_i = 0\) (and analogously for \(y\)) is also interesting: each customer “pulls” the site in their direction with a force of strength \(a_i\), regardless of their distance. At the optimum, all pulling forces cancel each other out. This explains the difference from the centre of gravity: there, a customer’s pulling force grows with their distance (the derivative of \(d_i^2\) is \(2 d_i\)), so that distant customers influence the result disproportionately.


5.3.3 Manhattan distances: the weighted median
If the Manhattan distance is used instead of the Euclidean distance, the structure of the problem changes fundamentally – to its advantage. The objective function \[
Z(x,y) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i \left(|x-u_i| + |y-v_i|\right)
= \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n a_i |x-u_i|}_{\text{depends only on } x} \; + \; \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n a_i |y-v_i|}_{\text{depends only on } y}
\] is additively separable in \(x\) and \(y\): the optimal \(x\) coordinate can be determined independently of the optimal \(y\) coordinate and vice versa. For each of the two partial sums, a classic result of optimisation applies: the sum of weighted absolute deviations \(\sum_i a_i |x - u_i|\) is minimised by the weighted median of the \(u_i\) – i.e. by the value at which at least half of the (cumulative, sorted by \(u_i\)) demand is reached.

Definition: Weighted median as the Steiner–Weber solution under Manhattan distance
Sort the customers in ascending order of their \(u_i\) coordinate and determine the cumulative demand \(A_j = \sum_{i=1}^{j} a_i\). The optimal \(x\) coordinate is the \(u_i\) coordinate of the first customer for whom \(A_j \geq \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\) holds. For \(y\), proceed analogously with the \(v_i\) coordinates.

Why the weighted median in particular? Consider what happens if the site is shifted a small distance \(\Delta\) to the right on the \(x\) axis. All customers to the left of the site move \(\Delta\) further away, all customers to the right of it move \(\Delta\) closer. The objective function thus changes by \(\Delta \cdot (A_{\text{left}} - A_{\text{right}})\), where \(A_{\text{left}}\) and \(A_{\text{right}}\) are the demand totals to the left and right of the site. A shift to the right pays off as long as there is more demand on the right than on the left. As soon as at least half of the total demand lies on the left, a further shift brings no further advantage — that is exactly the weighted median. It is remarkable that only the order of the customers on the axis and their demand quantities matter, not the exact distances: a customer who is very far away does not shift the median more strongly than a nearby customer with the same demand.

Code# Weighted median: smallest value at which the cumulative demand
# reaches at least half of the total demand
gewichteter_median <- function(werte, gewichte) {
  reihenfolge <- order(werte)          # determine sort index (ascending)
  werte <- werte[reihenfolge]          # sort values in this order
  gewichte <- gewichte[reihenfolge]    # sort weights in the same pattern

  kumuliert <- cumsum(gewichte)        # running (cumulative) sum of weights
  schwelle <- sum(gewichte) / 2        # half of total demand

  werte[which(kumuliert >= schwelle)[1]]  # first value that reaches the threshold
}

manhattan_lon <- gewichteter_median(filialen$lon, filialen$mu)
manhattan_lat <- gewichteter_median(filialen$lat, filialen$mu)
c(lon = manhattan_lon, lat = manhattan_lat)

    lon     lat 
 8.6512 50.0782 


The Manhattan solution \((x,y) \approx (8.6512; 50.0782)\) takes the longitude of Darmstadt on the \(x\) axis and the latitude of Wiesbaden on the \(y\) axis – a typical feature of the weighted median: on each coordinate axis individually, it always yields the value of an existing customer location, but because the \(x\) and \(y\) coordinates are determined independently of each other, it need not coincide overall with a single real store. The centre of gravity and the Weiszfeld optimum, by contrast, practically never coincide exactly with a customer location, since in their case both coordinates are averaged jointly from all stores. Which distance measure is appropriate is ultimately decided by the real transport structure in the sales area – not by the computational effort of the respective method.

section: 5.4 Geographic distances: reality check with the haversine formula
text:
5.4 Geographic distances: reality check with the haversine formula
The centre of gravity, the Weiszfeld algorithm and the weighted median implicitly assume that the coordinates \((u_i, v_i)\) are Cartesian coordinates in a plane on which Euclidean or Manhattan distances can be meaningfully interpreted. As announced above, we deliberately made this simplifying assumption throughout the section, even though latitude and longitude (WGS84) are actually coordinates on a curved surface of the earth, on which one degree of longitude corresponds to a different number of kilometres depending on the latitude. A naive Euclidean distance calculation based on degree coordinates would therefore be misleading at the latest for supra-regional distances – in the Rhine-Main area with its short distances, the error is small, but it should not go unquestioned.
For an exact comparison, the haversine formula is used, which calculates the great-circle distance – the shortest connection between two points on the surface of a sphere – from geographic coordinates:

Definition: Haversine distance
For two points with geographic latitude/longitude \((\varphi_1,\lambda_1)\) and \((\varphi_2,\lambda_2)\) (in radians), the great-circle distance is calculated as \[
d^{\text{hav}} = 2R \cdot \arctan2\!\left(\sqrt{a},\, \sqrt{1-a}\right),
\qquad
a = \sin^2\!\left(\frac{\Delta\varphi}{2}\right) + \cos(\varphi_1)\cos(\varphi_2)\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\Delta\lambda}{2}\right),
\] with \(R \approx 6{,}371\,\text{km}\) as the mean radius of the earth, \(\Delta\varphi = \varphi_2-\varphi_1\) and \(\Delta\lambda = \lambda_2-\lambda_1\).

The function haversine(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2) from R/scm_functions.R implements exactly this formula and returns the distance in kilometres. As a first application, we calculate the distance between the candidate site Wiesbaden-Erbenheim and the Frankfurt store:

Codehaversine(50.0632, 8.2999, 50.1109, 8.6821)

[1] 27.77917



5.4.1 Distance matrix between the candidate sites and the stores
The same function can be used to calculate the complete distance matrix between all three candidate sites and all six stores. Since haversine() is vectorised (it accepts vectors of equal length for lat1/lon1), we can apply it with sapply() once per store to the complete vector of the three site coordinates and directly obtain a matrix with one row per site and one column per store:

Code# sapply() over the six stores: for each store, haversine() is applied vectorised
# to all three sites at once -> 3x6 distance matrix
distanzmatrix <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(filialen)), function(j) {
  haversine(standorte$lat, standorte$lon, filialen$lat[j], filialen$lon[j])
})
rownames(distanzmatrix) <- standorte$Standort
colnames(distanzmatrix) <- filialen$Filiale
round(distanzmatrix, 1)

                    Wiesbaden Mainz Frankfurt Ruesselsheim Darmstadt Offenbach
Wiesbaden-Erbenheim       4.6   7.3      27.8         11.4      32.9      34.2
Mainz-Hechtsheim         12.4   3.5      32.5          9.5      28.5      37.9
Raunheim                 18.3  13.9      19.8          4.0      19.4      24.6


This distance matrix makes it possible to back up quantitatively the transport proximity that was only assessed qualitatively in the AHP. Multiplying the distance matrix by the demand vector of the stores – again via the matrix product %*% – yields, for each site, the demand-weighted total distance to all six stores:

Codegewichtete_gesamtdistanz <- distanzmatrix %*% filialen$mu
gewichtete_gesamtdistanz

                        [,1]
Wiesbaden-Erbenheim 17312.16
Mainz-Hechtsheim    18705.12
Raunheim            14652.44


With around 14652 box-kilometres, Raunheim has the lowest weighted total distance to the six stores, well ahead of Wiesbaden-Erbenheim (17312) and Mainz-Hechtsheim (18705). This purely quantitative indicator thus confirms the ranking that the AHP had derived for the criterion transport proximity (step 2) solely from qualitative pairwise comparisons – a nice example of how qualitative expert assessments and quantitative recalculation can mutually validate each other.

5.4.2 Reality check for the centre of gravity and the Weiszfeld optimum
Finally, we examine how realistic the two continuous optima from the previous section actually are when we drop the planar simplification made at the outset and calculate the true, spherical haversine distance to each store:

Codecog_dist <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(filialen)), function(j) {
  haversine(cog_lat, cog_lon, filialen$lat[j], filialen$lon[j])
})
weiszfeld_dist <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(filialen)), function(j) {
  haversine(ergebnis$y, ergebnis$x, filialen$lat[j], filialen$lon[j])
})

realitaetscheck <- tibble(
  Store = filialen$Filiale,
  Demand = filialen$mu,
  `CoG (km)` = round(cog_dist, 1),
  `Weiszfeld (km)` = round(weiszfeld_dist, 1)
)

  kable(align = "lccc") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

The picture is revealing: at around 6.9 km, the Weiszfeld optimum lies considerably closer to the highest-demand store, Frankfurt (280 boxes/day), than the centre of gravity at around 13.7 km – conversely, the Weiszfeld optimum moves noticeably further away than the CoG from the smaller stores further west, Wiesbaden and Mainz. The Weiszfeld algorithm thus deliberately “pulls” the site towards the large individual store in Frankfurt, whereas the centre of gravity, as a pure arithmetic mean, reacts less sensitively to individual large demand concentrations but, in return, also lies less close to them. This is not a general superiority of one method or the other, but a good starting point for discussion: how strongly a location method should react to individual large customers is ultimately a question of robustness against demand fluctuations and outliers – not solely a question of optimality within the model.
This brings us full circle to the three discrete candidate sites: neither the centre of gravity nor the Weiszfeld optimum lies on one of the three plots actually available – they merely show in which direction of the sales area a production facility would “ideally” shift. The actual location decision at SushiFresh therefore remains a discrete choice between the three candidates, for which the AHP in this chapter – narrowly – recommended Mainz-Hechtsheim, while Raunheim is clearly ahead on transport proximity. Whether this qualitative assessment is also confirmed by a pure cost analysis is examined in Chapter 6: there, with the warehouse location problem, we formulate a quantitative optimisation model that explicitly takes into account not only transport costs but also the fixed costs of the plots, and extends the set of candidates by two further sites – and which, as will become apparent, need not necessarily arrive at the same result as the qualitative evaluation carried out here.

title: 5  Facility Location Planning I – Qualitative and Continuous Methods
section: 5.5 Summary
text:
5.5 Summary
This chapter has contrasted two fundamentally different approaches to facility location planning, consistently using the example of SushiFresh GmbH and its search for a production site in the Rhine-Main area. Qualitative methods – the scoring model and the Analytic Hierarchy Process – evaluate a limited set of discrete alternatives (at SushiFresh: three candidate plots) on the basis of several criteria, including soft ones. The scoring model is simple to apply but suffers from the compensability of its additive structure, which in extreme cases can lead to alternatives with completely different profiles receiving the same overall utility value – as in the case example, in which all three sites achieved exactly the utility value 5.0. The AHP counters this weakness by deriving criteria and alternative weights from pairwise comparisons and by enabling explicit quality control of the expert assessments via the consistency index; in the case example – with a criteria matrix that was, however, not entirely consistent – it narrowly recommended the Mainz-Hechtsheim site.
Continuous methods go one step further and search for the optimal site not among given alternatives but as an arbitrary point in a plane. The centre of gravity provides a fast, closed-form approximate solution for this, which, however, only exactly minimises the squared objective function. The Weiszfeld algorithm iteratively solves the actual problem based on linear Euclidean distances and noticeably pulled the SushiFresh site towards the high-demand Frankfurt store. With Manhattan distances, the problem even simplifies to calculating a weighted median per coordinate. Finally, for large-scale geographic applications, the haversine formula provides a more realistic distance measure than the naive Euclidean distance on degree coordinates – and in the case example confirmed both the AHP ranking on transport proximity and the differences in robustness between the centre of gravity and the Weiszfeld optimum.
Both families of methods have in common that they either select the site from a given list of alternatives or determine it as an arbitrary point in space. In practice, however, the set of realistic sites is often neither completely freely selectable nor limited to a few alternatives preselected by hand, but consists of a larger but finite set of eligible plots or buildings. For this case – discrete facility location planning with warehouse location models and network planning heuristics – Chapter 6 extends the methodological toolkit with exact and heuristic optimisation methods. There, we return to the SushiFresh case study and examine whether the narrow AHP recommendation in favour of Mainz-Hechtsheim is also confirmed by an explicit cost calculation.

Review questions

Explain the five-step procedure of the scoring model and name two of its methodological weaknesses.
Why can alternatives with completely different strength–weakness profiles achieve the same overall utility value in the scoring model?
Describe the five steps of the AHP. What role does the pairwise comparison matrix play?
How is the consistency index (CI) of a pairwise comparison matrix calculated, and below which threshold of the consistency ratio (CR) is a matrix usually considered sufficiently consistent?
Derive the formula for the centre of gravity from the minimisation of the weighted squared Euclidean distances.
Why does the Weiszfeld algorithm generally provide a better (lower-cost) solution than the centre of gravity, even though both are based on Euclidean distances? What does this mean specifically for the Frankfurt store in the SushiFresh example?
How does determining the optimal site under Manhattan distances differ from determining it under Euclidean distances?
Why is the direct application of Euclidean distances to geographic coordinates (latitude/longitude) problematic, and what alternative does the haversine formula offer?
In the case example, the AHP narrowly recommends the Mainz-Hechtsheim site. Give two reasons why a purely cost-based analysis (as in Chapter 6) could arrive at a different result.
In the R code, change the comparison “transport proximity versus skilled labour” from 2 to 1/2. How do the consistency ratio and the ranking of the sites change? Interpret the result.

title: 6  Facility Location Planning II – Discrete Network Planning Models
text:
6.1 From continuous to discrete facility location planning
In the previous chapter you learnt how to use the centre-of-gravity approach and the Weiszfeld algorithm to determine an arbitrary point in the plane that minimises the weighted distances to a set of demand points. In the example of SushiFresh GmbH – a regional producer of fresh sushi boxes in the Rhine-Main area that supplies six supermarket stores every day – the optimal point calculated in this way lay between Raunheim and Frankfurt, shifted clearly towards Frankfurt, the store with the highest demand. This continuous view of location choice is analytically elegant but of limited help in business practice: SushiFresh cannot build a production facility at exactly the calculated coordinates but has to choose among the commercial plots, halls or existing properties that are actually available. Planning law, land prices, transport links and food hygiene requirements restrict the set of realistically usable locations to a finite set of alternatives known in advance. This is precisely the starting point of discrete facility location planning: instead of an optimisation problem over the entire plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the focus is on a selection decision from a fixed list of potential locations.
In Chapter 5 the location question for SushiFresh was already addressed twice: first, a qualitative assessment of three candidate locations was carried out using the AHP (Analytic Hierarchy Process) – with the result that Mainz-Hechtsheim came out narrowly ahead of Raunheim, although the criteria weights were based on judgements that were not entirely consistent. Subsequently, the centre-of-gravity/Weiszfeld approach delivered a continuous optimal point in the middle of the sales area. This chapter poses the location question a third time – now on the basis of hard cost figures: fixed costs for operating a location and variable transport costs to the stores supplied. As we shall see, a purely cost-based, discrete analysis arrives at a different result from the qualitative pre-selection – and precisely this tension between the two methods is discussed explicitly at the end of the chapter.
Discrete location decisions are always embedded in a larger supply chain network, which can be roughly divided into the stages of procurement, production, distribution and sales. At each of these stages, nodes (supplier plants, production facilities, warehouses, cross-docking points) can be opened, closed or connected with one another; in this context one also speaks of network design. The lecture emphasises that in practice usually only a section of the overall network is considered: specific locations are selected at one or two stages while the remaining stages are held fixed. Accordingly, this chapter concentrates on the question of which production and distribution locations SushiFresh should operate and which store should be supplied from which location. The models presented can, however, be transferred directly to other network stages.
We approach discrete facility location planning in two steps. First, we consider the special case in which the locations are already fixed and only the delivery quantities have to be optimally allocated to the stores – the classical transportation problem. We then extend the model to include the actual location decision: the warehouse location problem (WLP), in which both the question “where?” and the question “how much to where?” have to be answered simultaneously.
crumbs: 6  Facility Location Planning II – Discrete Network Planning Models

title: 6  Facility Location Planning II – Discrete Network Planning Models
text:
Definition: Discrete facility location planning
In discrete facility location planning, the subset of a finite set of predefined potential locations is selected that minimises a given target value (usually the sum of fixed location costs and variable transport costs). In contrast to continuous facility location planning, the solution space is no longer continuous but combinatorial: every possible subset of locations represents a feasible solution.

title: 6  Facility Location Planning II – Discrete Network Planning Models
section: 6.3 The classical transportation problem
text:
6.3 The classical transportation problem
Let us first assume that SushiFresh – hypothetically, as a starting scenario before the actual location decision – already operates all five locations simultaneously and “only” has to decide which store is supplied from which location and with what quantity. The locations have limited daily production capacities which in total correspond exactly to the total demand of all six stores:

Codeangebot   <- c(S1 = 200, S2 = 150, S3 = 250, S4 = 120, S5 = 125)   # boxes/day
nachfrage <- setNames(filialen_fall$mu, filialen_fall$ID)          # boxes/day

c(Supply = sum(angebot), Demand = sum(nachfrage))

Supply Demand 
   845    845 


Five sources (supply of the locations) and six sinks (demand of the stores) – the classical transportation problem.

Definition: Transportation problem
In the (classical) transportation problem, \(m\) sources \(i \in I\) with supply quantities \(s_i\) and \(n\) sinks \(j \in J\) with demand quantities \(a_j\) are given. For each connection \((i,j)\), transport costs \(c_{ij}\) are incurred per unit transported. The task is to find a cost-minimal allocation of the supply quantities to the demand quantities. The problem is called balanced if \(\sum_i s_i = \sum_j a_j\) holds; otherwise it is unbalanced.

Formally, the corresponding linear optimisation model with the transport quantities \(x_{ij} \geq 0\) as decision variables reads:
\[
\begin{align}
\min \quad & \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{j \in J} c_{ij} \cdot x_{ij} \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & \sum_{j \in J} x_{ij} \leq s_i & \forall i \in I \quad &\rightarrow \text{supply constraint} \\
& \sum_{i \in I} x_{ij} = a_j & \forall j \in J \quad &\rightarrow \text{meet demand exactly} \\
& x_{ij} \geq 0 & \forall (i,j) &\quad \rightarrow \text{non-negativity}
\end{align}
\]
Since all constraints and the objective function are linear in \(x_{ij}\), this is a pure linear optimisation problem (not an MILP) – the optimal solution always lies at a vertex of the solution polyhedron, and specialised, very efficient solution methods exist.

In depth (theory): Why transportation problems yield integer solutions “by themselves”
The constraint matrix of the transportation problem has a special structure: each variable \(x_{ij}\) appears in exactly two constraints – once in the supply row of \(i\) and once in the demand row of \(j\) – each time with the coefficient 1. Matrices with this structure are totally unimodular, i.e. every square submatrix has the determinant 0, +1 or −1. By Cramer’s rule it follows that every vertex of the solution polyhedron is integer, provided the supply and demand quantities are integer. In practice this means: although the transportation problem is solved as an LP with continuous variables, one automatically obtains integer transport quantities – there is no need to round “half boxes” afterwards.
A second useful property concerns the number of positive transport quantities: a basic solution of a balanced transportation problem has at most \(m + n - 1\) positive variables. With five locations and six stores, at most ten of the thirty possible connections are therefore used – most stores are supplied by exactly one location, and only a few are “split” between two locations. The opening procedures below generate precisely such basic solutions.

Historically, so-called tableau methods were developed for transportation problems; they build on the simplex idea but exploit the special structure. Two classical opening procedures that construct an initial feasible solution are the north-west corner method and Vogel’s approximation method.
The north-west corner method is extremely simple: one starts in the “north-west corner” of the tableau (row 1, column 1), supplies as much as possible there, deletes the row or column thereby exhausted and repeats the procedure for the remaining matrix. Its great advantage is its simplicity; its drawback: the costs \(c_{ij}\) are not taken into account at all when choosing the cells. The method therefore always delivers a feasible, but often economically poor, starting solution.
Vogel’s approximation method (VAM) improves on this by giving priority in each step to the row or column where a “wrong” decision would be most expensive. To do this, a penalty cost difference (penalty) is calculated for each row and each column: the difference between the two lowest costs in that row or column. A large difference means: if the cheapest cell is not chosen here, it becomes disproportionately expensive (opportunity cost of the second-best choice). The basic idea can be summarised as follows:
# Core idea of Vogel's approximation method (simplified):
# Repeat as long as supply and demand remain open:
#   1. For each active row/column, calculate the penalty cost difference
#      = difference between the two lowest costs in that
#        row or column
#   2. Choose the row/column with the LARGEST penalty cost difference
#   3. In it, supply the cheapest cell with the maximum possible
#      quantity (= min(remaining supply, remaining demand))
#   4. Update remaining supply/demand; if a row/column is
#      exhausted, it is removed from further consideration

R aside: Matrices as cost and transport tableaus
So far you have mainly encountered tabular data as a data.frame/tibble, in which each column represents a named attribute vector with distinct content (e.g. place, longitude, demand). A cost or transport tableau, by contrast, is a homogeneous, purely numerical table in which what matters is not column names in the substantive sense but the position (row \(i\), column \(j\)). The R data type matrix (matrix()) is the natural choice for this – as with kosten_mat above. Rows and columns can be named via dimnames and then addressed directly:

Codekosten_mat["S3", ]          # all cost rates of Raunheim

     C1      C2      C3      C4      C5      C6 
0.48168 0.27202 0.17036 0.54650 0.44772 0.12592 

Codekosten_mat[, "C3"]          # costs of supplying Frankfurt from each location

     S1      S2      S3      S4      S5 
0.47474 0.59168 0.17036 0.89392 0.90576 

Codeapply(kosten_mat, 2, which.min)   # per store: row index of the cheapest location

C1 C2 C3 C4 C5 C6 
 2  3  3  4  5  5 


After solving, rowSums() and colSums() make it very easy to check whether a calculated allocation matrix is feasible: the row sums must equal the supply, the column sums the demand.

The function vogels_approximation() from R/scm_functions.R implements the procedure outlined above in full, including automatic balancing via a dummy location or dummy store if supply and demand do not match:

Codevam_ergebnis <- vogels_approximation(
  cost_mat = kosten_mat,
  supply   = angebot,
  demand   = nachfrage,
  verbose  = FALSE
)

vam_ergebnis$allocation

S1   0 90  30  0   0 80
S2 120 30   0  0   0  0
S3   0  0 250  0   0  0
S4   0 30   0 90   0  0
S5   0  0   0  0 110 15

Coderound(vam_ergebnis$total_cost, 2)   # transport costs in EUR/day

[1] 222.35

Code# Feasibility check
rowSums(vam_ergebnis$allocation) == angebot

  S1   S2   S3   S4   S5 
TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE 

CodecolSums(vam_ergebnis$allocation) == nachfrage

  C1   C2   C3   C4   C5   C6 
TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE 


The allocation matrix shows an economically plausible picture: the stores are mainly supplied by the nearby locations, and only where a location has already exhausted its capacity is a store split between two locations. Total costs amount to €222.35 per day. Since VAM is an opening heuristic, this result need not be the optimal solution. How good it is can be checked by additionally solving the transportation problem exactly as an LP (with the package ompr, which is introduced in detail further below):

Codelibrary(ompr)
library(ompr.roi)
library(ROI.plugin.glpk)

m <- nrow(kosten_mat); n <- ncol(kosten_mat)

tp_modell <- MIPModel() |>
  add_variable(x[i, j], i = 1:m, j = 1:n, type = "continuous", lb = 0) |>
  set_objective(sum_expr(kosten_mat[i, j] * x[i, j], i = 1:m, j = 1:n), "min") |>
  add_constraint(sum_expr(x[i, j], j = 1:n) <= angebot[i], i = 1:m) |>
  add_constraint(sum_expr(x[i, j], i = 1:m) == nachfrage[j], j = 1:n)

tp_loesung <- solve_model(tp_modell, with_ROI(solver = "glpk"))
tp_opt     <- objective_value(tp_loesung)

c(VAM = round(vam_ergebnis$total_cost, 2), Optimum = round(tp_opt, 2),
  Deviation_percent = round((vam_ergebnis$total_cost / tp_opt - 1) * 100, 2))

              VAM           Optimum Deviation_percent 
           222.35            222.35              0.00 


In this example, VAM actually finds the optimal solution straight away – this is not guaranteed, but it happens frequently with small instances because the penalty cost logic deliberately avoids the expensive wrong decisions. The transportation problem, however, assumes that the set of supplying locations is already fixed. It is precisely this assumption that is relaxed in the next section.

title: 6  Facility Location Planning II – Discrete Network Planning Models
section: 6.4 The warehouse location problem
text:
6.4 The warehouse location problem
In practice, it usually has to be clarified not only how stores are supplied but also from which locations deliveries should be made at all. For SushiFresh this is the actual strategic question: is it worth operating several locations simultaneously, or is consolidation onto one or two locations cheaper? Every location opening entails a fixed annual cost burden, regardless of how much is later actually delivered via this location. This decision problem is called the warehouse location problem (WLP) or also the uncapacitated facility location problem if – as here – no capacity limits per location are assumed.

Definition: Warehouse location problem
Let there be a set of potential locations \(i \in I\) with annual opening costs \(f_i\) and a set of customer locations \(j \in J\) with demand quantities \(a_j\). For each possible transport connection \((i,j) \in E \subseteq I \times J\), transport costs \(c_{ij}\) are incurred per unit supplied. The task is to find the subset of locations to be opened and the corresponding assignment of customers to locations that minimises the sum of opening and transport costs.

In contrast to the transportation problem, the WLP now contains two types of decision variables: a binary location decision \(y_i \in \{0,1\}\) (location \(i\) is opened or not) and, as before, the continuous transport quantities \(x_{ij} \geq 0\). The complete model reads:
\[
\min \rightarrow \sum_{i \in I} y_i \cdot f_i + \sum_{(i,j) \in E} x_{ij} \cdot c_{ij}
\]
subject to the constraints
\[
\begin{align}
  \sum_{(i,j) \in E} x_{ij} &= a_j          & \forall j \in J      &\quad\rightarrow \text{satisfy demand completely} \\
  x_{ij}                    &\leq y_i \cdot a_j & \forall (i,j) \in E &\quad\rightarrow \text{only transports from opened locations} \\
  x_{ij}                    &\geq 0          & \forall (i,j) \in E &\quad\rightarrow \text{transport quantities non-negative} \\
  y_i                       &\in \{0,1\}     & \forall i \in I     &\quad\rightarrow \text{location is opened or not}
\end{align}
\]
The second constraint is the decisive difference from the pure transportation problem: as long as \(y_i = 0\) (location \(i\) not opened), it forces all associated transport quantities \(x_{ij}\) to zero – a closed location cannot supply any store. Only when \(y_i = 1\) is set is \(x_{ij}\) permitted up to at most the full demand \(a_j\). Because both continuous and binary variables appear in the same model, this is a mixed-integer linear optimisation model (mixed-integer linear program, MILP) – a considerably more difficult problem class than the pure LP of the transportation problem.

In depth (theory): Structure of the optimal solution and “strong” formulations
Because the WLP has no capacity limits, its optimal solution has a simple structure: as soon as it is fixed which locations are open, each store is supplied entirely from the cheapest open location. Splitting a store between several locations can never be better, since every box should be transported on the cheapest available connection. The real difficulty of the problem therefore lies solely in the combinatorial selection of the set of locations – with \(|I|\) candidates there are \(2^{|I|}-1\) non-empty subsets. The add and drop heuristics and the helper function .wlp_cost() exploit precisely this observation.
For exact solution with an MILP solver, the formulation of the linking constraint is important. Instead of the disaggregated form \(x_{ij} \leq y_i \cdot a_j\) used here (one constraint per connection), one could also write an aggregated form \(\sum_j x_{ij} \leq y_i \cdot \sum_j a_j\) (one constraint per location). Both formulations have the same integer solutions. Solvers, however, work with the LP relaxation, in which \(y_i\) may take values between 0 and 1. In the aggregated form, a very small \(y_i\) then suffices to open a location “a little” and supply all stores through it – the relaxation provides a weak lower bound, and the branch-and-bound procedure has to search many branches. The disaggregated form, by contrast, requires \(y_i \geq x_{ij}/a_j\) for each individual connection and is therefore much closer to the integer solution; this is referred to as a strong formulation. For the uncapacitated WLP, the LP relaxation of the disaggregated form is often already integer (Daskin 2013).

Unlike the transportation problem in the previous section, we calculate the WLP on an annual basis: the fixed costs \(f_i\) are annual values, and demand must also be scaled up from the daily to the annual level. The numerical example in the lecture uses the simplified factor 1,000 for this (\(a_j = 1{,}000 \cdot \mu_j\)). We adopt this assumption for now and check at the end of the chapter how sensitively the result reacts to a more realistic scaling-up with 365 sales days. Before we compile the data, it is worth looking at another central R concept: the list.

R aside: Lists as a flexible data structure
A vector in R can only hold elements of one data type, and a data.frame/tibble requires all columns to have the same length. Often, however, one wants to manage objects of different structure, length or type together – for instance the name of a location (text), its coordinates (a vector of length 2), its fixed costs (a number) and a status (logical). This is exactly what the list (list()) is intended for: a container whose elements may be any – including heterogeneous – R objects.
A named element is accessed either with the dollar sign $name or with double square brackets [["name"]] or [[position]]. The difference from single square brackets [ ] is important: liste[1] returns a sub-list with one element, liste[[1]] returns the content of that element itself.

Code# A single piece of location information as a list
standort_info <- list(
  name        = "Wiesbaden-Erbenheim",
  koordinaten = c(lon = 8.2999, lat = 50.0632),  # vector as element
  fixkosten   = 36000,
  aktiv       = TRUE
)

standort_info$name                     # access via $

[1] "Wiesbaden-Erbenheim"

Codestandort_info[["fixkosten"]]           # access via [[ ]] with name

[1] 36000

Codestandort_info[["koordinaten"]]["lat"]  # nested access

    lat 
50.0632 


Lists are not only useful for input – the return values of many R functions are also lists as soon as more than one result is to be returned. We already made use of this in the previous section: vogels_approximation() returns a list with the fields allocation (matrix), total_cost (number) and balanced (logical). Likewise, add_heuristic_wlp() and drop_heuristic_wlp(), which we use further below, return their result as a list with the fields open_warehouses, fixed_cost, transport_cost, total_cost and assignment.

For the actual calculation we need the fixed costs and the annual demand as named vectors, as well as the cost matrix kosten_mat:

Codefixkosten_vec  <- setNames(standorte_fall$Fixkosten, standorte_fall$ID)   # EUR/year
nachfrage_jahr <- setNames(filialen_fall$mu * 1000, filialen_fall$ID)     # boxes/year (factor 1,000)

fixkosten_vec

36000 42000 52000 48000 40000 

Codenachfrage_jahr

120000 150000 280000  90000 110000  95000 


Five locations mean \(2^5 - 1 = 31\) possible non-empty location configurations – small enough to evaluate them all in the next R aside.

R aside: purrr::map() – applying a function to every element
Often one wants to apply the same calculation to every element of a list or vector – for example: “calculate the total costs for every possible combination of locations”. Instead of writing a for loop for this (Chapter 5), the tidyverse package purrr offers the map() family of functions. map(x, f) applies the function f to every element of x and returns a list; map_dbl(x, f) does the same but requires f to return a single number (double) per element, and then automatically simplifies the result to a numeric vector. It is the direct relative of sapply() from Chapter 5, with the advantage that the return type is clearly fixed and errors therefore become apparent earlier.
We first generate all non-empty subsets of the five locations with the base R function combn() and then evaluate them with map_dbl() and the helper function .wlp_cost() from scm_functions.R, which, for a given set of open locations, calculates the optimal store assignment (each store to the cheapest open location) and the resulting total costs:

Coden_I <- length(fixkosten_vec)

# All non-empty subsets of {1, ..., 5}: combn(5, k) returns all
# combinations of size k, unlist(..., recursive = FALSE) merges them into
# a single list
alle_teilmengen <- unlist(
  lapply(1:n_I, function(k) combn(n_I, k, simplify = FALSE)),
  recursive = FALSE
)
length(alle_teilmengen)  # 2^5 - 1 = 31

The ranking is revealing. First, the best solutions lie very close together: the combination Mainz-Hechtsheim + Raunheim and the single location Raunheim are only a few thousand euros per year more expensive than the optimum. Second, Raunheim appears in all the leading solutions – the location with the highest investment costs is the backbone of every good network because, according to the cost matrix, it reaches the high-demand Frankfurt store and most of the other stores most cheaply. title: 6  Facility Location Planning II – Discrete Network Planning Models
section: 6.5 Exact solution with ompr
text:
6.5 Exact solution with ompr
The WLP can be solved exactly as an MILP with specialised solvers without evaluating all subsets individually. In R, the package ompr (Optimization Modeling Package for R) handles the algebraic formulation of the model; the actual numerical solution is delegated via ompr.roi to a solver – here glpk, the free GNU Linear Programming Kit. The appeal of ompr lies in the fact that the objective function and constraints can be translated almost literally from the mathematical formulation into R code.

R aside: Algebraic optimisation modelling with ompr
So far we have solved optimisation problems (centre of gravity, Weiszfeld, Vogel’s method) using tailor-made algorithms. ompr takes a more generic approach: the model is described declaratively (variables, objective function, constraints) and the search for a solution is left to a universal solver. The workflow is divided into six steps:


MIPModel() – create an empty model object,

add_variable() – define decision variables with type (binary, continuous, integer) and index set,

set_objective() – formulate the objective function (sum_expr() forms sums over index sets, analogous to \(\sum\) in mathematical notation),

add_constraint() – formulate constraints, likewise indexed,

solve_model() – pass the model to a specific solver,

get_solution() – extract the optimal values of the decision variables from the result object.

In the following code, y[i] corresponds to the binary location variable \(y_i\) and x[i,j] to the transport quantity variable \(x_{ij}\). sum_expr(f[i] * y[i], i = 1:n_I) forms exactly the expression \(\sum_{i\in I} f_i \cdot y_i\); the two add_constraint() calls implement the demand and linking constraints of the WLP model.

Coden_J  <- length(nachfrage_jahr)
f    <- fixkosten_vec     # opening costs f_i (EUR/year)
a    <- nachfrage_jahr    # demand a_j (boxes/year)
c_ij <- kosten_mat        # transport costs (EUR/box)

modell <- MIPModel() |>
  # Decision variable y_i: open location i (1) or not (0)
  add_variable(y[i], i = 1:n_I, type = "binary") |>
  # Decision variable x_ij: transport quantity from location i to store j
  add_variable(x[i, j], i = 1:n_I, j = 1:n_J, type = "continuous", lb = 0) |>
  # Objective function: minimise opening costs + transport costs
  set_objective(
    sum_expr(f[i] * y[i], i = 1:n_I) +
      sum_expr(c_ij[i, j] * x[i, j], i = 1:n_I, j = 1:n_J),
    sense = "min") |>
  # C1: satisfy the demand of each store j completely
  add_constraint(sum_expr(x[i, j], i = 1:n_I) == a[j], j = 1:n_J) |>
  # C2: transport only from opened locations (x_ij <= y_i * a_j)
  add_constraint(x[i, j] <= y[i] * a[j], i = 1:n_I, j = 1:n_J)

ergebnis_milp <- solve_model(modell, with_ROI(solver = "glpk", verbose = FALSE))



After solving, we use get_solution() to extract the optimal values of the variables \(y_i\) and \(x_{ij}\), and objective_value() to obtain the optimal objective function value \(Z^*\):

Codey_sol <- get_solution(ergebnis_milp, y[i])
x_sol <- get_solution(ergebnis_milp, x[i, j])

offene_idx       <- y_sol$i[y_sol$value > 0.5]
offene_standorte <- standorte_fall$Standort[offene_idx]

title: 6  Facility Location Planning II – Discrete Network Planning Models
section: 6.6 Heuristic solution methods: add and drop heuristics
text:
6.6 Heuristic solution methods: add and drop heuristics
Despite the power of modern MILP solvers, the WLP remains an NP-hard problem: in the worst case, the computing time required for an exact solution grows exponentially with the number of locations and customers. For very large practical instances – a Germany-wide store network with hundreds of candidate locations and thousands of stores, possibly with further constraints (capacities, multi-stage networks) – even a good solver can run into time or memory limits. In such cases, constructive heuristics are often the practicable route to a usable, though not necessarily optimal, solution.
The basic idea of both heuristics presented below is greedy: starting from a feasible initial configuration, in each step exactly the change that reduces total costs the most is made; the procedure stops as soon as no further improvement is possible. Stores are always assigned to the cheapest open location (\(\sigma(j) = \arg\min_{i \in S} c_{ij}\)), so that the total costs of a set of locations \(S\) can be calculated unambiguously as
\[Z(S) = \underbrace{\sum_{i \in S} f_i}_{\text{opening}} + \underbrace{\sum_{j \in J} \min_{i \in S} c_{ij} \cdot a_j}_{\text{transport}}.\]
The add heuristic starts with the empty set \(S = \emptyset\) and in each step adds the location \(i^*\) whose opening reduces total costs the most: \(\Delta_i = Z(S) - Z(S \cup \{i\})\), \(i^* = \arg\max_{i \notin S} \Delta_i\). If \(\Delta_{i^*} > 0\), \(i^*\) is opened; otherwise the procedure terminates. In economic terms, adding a location is worthwhile precisely when the transport cost savings it achieves are greater than its opening costs. Transport costs fall from step to step, while fixed costs rise.
The drop heuristic takes the opposite route: it starts with all locations open (\(S = I\)) and in each step closes the location whose closure reduces total costs the most (\(\Delta_i = Z(S) - Z(S \setminus \{i\})\)), until here too no further improvement is possible. A location is closed if its fixed costs are higher than the transport costs incurred because its stores have to be reassigned to the next-best location.

Add heuristic

\(S = \emptyset\) (costs \(\infty\))

\(S = I\) (all fixed costs incurred)

constructive (building up)

Effort per step

Tendency
rather few locations
rather more locations



Both variants are implemented in R/scm_functions.R as add_heuristic_wlp() and drop_heuristic_wlp() respectively (including the internal cost calculation via .wlp_cost()). With verbose = TRUE they log each step:

Codenames(fixkosten_vec) <- standorte_fall$Standort   # names for a readable log

add_ergebnis <- add_heuristic_wlp(
  fixed_costs        = fixkosten_vec,
  transport_cost_mat = kosten_mat,
  demand             = nachfrage_jahr,
  verbose            = TRUE
)

[Add iter 1] Open Raunheim | Total cost: 308702
[Add iter 2] Open Wiesbaden-Erbenheim | Total cost: 301718

Coderound(add_ergebnis$total_cost)

[1] 301718


In the first step, the add heuristic opens Raunheim – the location that, on its own, incurs the lowest total costs of all single locations. In the second step, Wiesbaden-Erbenheim is added because the transport cost savings for the Wiesbaden store exceed the additional fixed costs. After that, no further location can reduce costs.

Codedrop_ergebnis <- drop_heuristic_wlp(
  fixed_costs        = fixkosten_vec,
  transport_cost_mat = kosten_mat,
  demand             = nachfrage_jahr,
  verbose            = TRUE
)

[Drop iter 1] Close Mainz-Hechtsheim | New total cost: 355549
[Drop iter 2] Close Frankfurt-Hoechst | New total cost: 326583
[Drop iter 3] Close Neu-Isenburg | New total cost: 301718

Coderound(drop_ergebnis$total_cost)

[1] 301718


The drop heuristic starts with all five locations open and successively closes Mainz-Hechtsheim, Frankfurt-Höchst and Neu-Isenburg – in each case the location whose fixed costs generate the least “transport benefit”. What remains are Wiesbaden-Erbenheim and Raunheim: here the add and drop heuristics independently converge on the same, demonstrably optimal solution. This is by no means a matter of course – with other cost structures, the two procedures can end in different, suboptimal solutions – but here it shows how clearly the cost structure of the case example points to this configuration.

Codevergleich <- tibble(

The figure shows the typical U-shape of total costs plotted against the number of locations – the same trade-off logic that was introduced in Chapter 3 as the “decision on the number of warehouses”: with each additional location, transport costs fall while fixed costs rise. The minimum lies at two locations, but the curve is very flat in the vicinity of the minimum.
For practice this means: the add and drop heuristics should – where possible – be run in parallel and compared with the result of an exact method (or at least a known lower bound) before a location decision with long-term binding effect is taken. Especially for distribution locations, which can only be revised at great expense, a reliable quality measure (the gap to the optimum) is indispensable (Chopra and Meindl 2025).

section: 6.7 How robust is the solution? A sensitivity analysis
text:
6.7 How robust is the solution? A sensitivity analysis
The flat cost curve suggests that the optimal solution could react sensitively to assumptions. The most important assumption of the numerical example is the scaling-up of daily to annual demand by the factor 1,000. If SushiFresh sells on 365 days a year, the actual annual quantity – and hence the weight of transport costs relative to fixed costs – would be considerably smaller. With map_dfr() the optimum can be determined for different scaling factors:

Codebestes_netz <- function(faktor) {
  a_tmp  <- filialen_fall$mu * faktor
  kosten <- map_dbl(alle_teilmengen, ~ .wlp_cost(.x, fixkosten_vec, kosten_mat, a_tmp)$total)
  S      <- alle_teilmengen[[which.min(kosten)]]
  tibble(Days_per_year = faktor,
         Optimal_network = paste(standorte_fall$Standort[S], collapse = " + "),
         Total_costs = round(min(kosten)))
}

map_dfr(c(250, 300, 365, 500, 750, 1000), bestes_netz) |>
  kbl(format.args = list(big.mark = ",", decimal.mark = ".")) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)

section: 6.8 Qualitative vs. quantitative location assessment
text:
6.8 Qualitative vs. quantitative location assessment
At this point it is worth looking back at Chapter 5: there, the AHP analysis narrowly favoured Mainz-Hechtsheim among the three original candidates – mainly because of the very good rating for the availability of skilled labour there. The quantitative cost optimisation carried out in this chapter comes to a clearly different conclusion: Mainz-Hechtsheim does not appear in any of the best solutions; the cost-optimal choice is Raunheim (alone or together with Wiesbaden-Erbenheim).

Codemap_dfr(1:3, function(i) {
  res <- .wlp_cost(i, fixkosten_vec, kosten_mat, nachfrage_jahr)
  tibble(Location = standorte_fall$Standort[i], Fixed_costs = res$fixed,
         Transport_costs = round(res$transport), Total_costs = round(res$total))
}) |>
  kbl(caption = "The three original candidates as single locations (factor 1,000)",
      format.args = list(big.mark = ",", decimal.mark = ".")) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)

The reason for the discrepancy lies in the transport costs: Mainz-Hechtsheim lies on the western edge of the sales area, whereas the bulk of demand (above all Frankfurt) arises further east. The transport costs of a single location at Mainz-Hechtsheim are therefore far higher than those of Raunheim – a disadvantage that neither the lower fixed costs nor the good availability of skilled labour can offset, as long as the latter is not valued in euros.
This observation is not a contradiction but illustrates the different function of the two methods in the decision-making process: the AHP is suitable for an initial pre-selection based on criteria that are difficult to quantify and partly soft, and for incorporating different stakeholder perspectives. It does not, however, replace a robust cost optimisation as soon as hard figures are available. Conversely, a pure cost optimisation falls short if aspects that are difficult to monetise are ignored: if hardly any suitable skilled workers could actually be found in Raunheim, this would be reflected in higher personnel costs, quality problems or start-up difficulties of which the WLP knows nothing. In practice, the two methods complement each other: qualitative methods to reduce the search space and to check knock-out criteria, quantitative optimisation models for the final, cost-based decision between the remaining candidates.

Case study: Interim result for SushiFresh
The WLP recommends a central location in Raunheim, possibly supplemented by a second location in Wiesbaden-Erbenheim. Since the two-location solution in the numerical example is only around €6,984/year cheaper than the single location Raunheim, and is even more expensive with realistic scaling-up, there is much to be said for consolidating production in a central kitchen in Raunheim. However, the WLP ignores one important effect: the inventories that have to be held at each location as a safeguard against demand fluctuations. Precisely this question – how much safety stock does centralised supply save compared with decentralised supply? – is examined in Chapter 7. It provides an additional, weighty argument in favour of consolidation.

title: 6  Facility Location Planning II – Discrete Network Planning Models
section: 6.9 Summary
text:
6.9 Summary
This chapter has made the transition from continuous to discrete facility location planning: instead of an arbitrary point in the plane, a subset is sought from a finite list of predefined candidate locations. As a methodological starting point, we became acquainted with the classical transportation problem, in which the supplying locations are already fixed and only the transport flows have to be determined at minimum cost; its constraint matrix is totally unimodular, so that the LP solution is automatically integer. Vogel’s approximation method delivers a good starting solution in a few steps by giving priority to supplying the row or column with the largest penalty cost difference.
The warehouse location problem extends this model to include the actual location decision: a binary variable \(y_i\) per location decides on opening or not opening, linked to the transport quantities \(x_{ij}\) via the constraint \(x_{ij} \leq y_i \cdot a_j\). Because both binary and continuous variables occur, this is an MILP that can be solved exactly with ompr in a few lines of code closely modelled on the mathematical formulation. The SushiFresh example showed that the centrally located Raunheim site forms the backbone of every good network despite having the highest investment costs; whether a second location in Wiesbaden-Erbenheim is added depends – as the sensitivity analysis showed – on the scaling-up of demand. The qualitative AHP recommendation (Mainz-Hechtsheim) was not confirmed by the cost optimisation, which underlines the need for both methods in the decision-making process. Since the WLP is NP-hard, constructive add and drop heuristics are a practicable way out for large instances – in the case example both found the global optimum, although this is not a generally valid property of these methods.
On the R side, this chapter has introduced you to four new building blocks: lists as a flexible container for heterogeneous data and function results; purrr::map()/map_dbl()/map_dfr() for compactly applying a function to every element of a list; matrices as the natural representation of position-based tableaus, with rowSums()/colSums() for consistency checks; and algebraic optimisation modelling with ompr.

Review questions

How does discrete facility location planning differ from continuous facility location planning, and why is the discrete variant more realistic for most practical location decisions?
Formulate the objective function and constraints of the classical transportation problem. What does it mean if a transportation problem is “unbalanced”, and how does vogels_approximation() deal with this?
Explain the basic idea of Vogel’s approximation method. Why does it usually deliver better starting solutions than the north-west corner method?
Why does the LP solution of a transportation problem with integer supply and demand quantities automatically yield integer transport quantities?
Which additional decision variable does the warehouse location problem contain compared with the transportation problem, and what role does the constraint \(x_{ij} \leq y_i \cdot a_j\) play? Why is it preferable to the aggregated form \(\sum_j x_{ij} \leq y_i \sum_j a_j\)?
Describe the add and drop heuristics in your own words. Under what condition is it worthwhile in the add heuristic to open a further location?
What is meant by the “gap to the optimum”, and why is it an important indicator for heuristic location decisions?
Explain the difference between a list (list()) and a data.frame/tibble. Give an example from this chapter in which an R function sensibly returns its result as a list.
Why, in the SushiFresh example, is one location optimal with 365 sales days, whereas two locations are optimal with 1,000 “days”? Argue on the basis of the structure of the objective function.
The AHP analysis (Chapter 5) favours Mainz-Hechtsheim, the WLP analysis Raunheim. Explain the discrepancy and discuss how the two methods can be sensibly combined in practice.

Daskin, Mark S. 2013. Network and Discrete Location: Models, Algorithms, and Applications. 2nd ed. Wiley.


Drezner, Zvi, and Horst W. Hamacher, eds. 2002. Facility Location: Applications and Theory. Springer.


Günther, Hans-Otto, and Horst Tempelmeier. 2012. Produktion und Logistik. 9th ed. Springer-Lehrbuch. Springer.

title: 7  Uncertainty in Supply Chains and Pooling
text:
7.1 The Nature of Uncertainty in Supply Chains
Chapters 5 and 6 showed how facilities and networks are planned under the assumption of known, fixed demands. In reality, this assumption is almost never met: demand fluctuates from period to period, lead times vary, and capacities have to be fixed long in advance, before it is even known how much will actually be needed. This chapter deals with how supply chains cope with this uncertainty — through appropriate quantification, through safety stocks and, as a central design principle, through pooling: the bundling of capacities or inventories so that demand fluctuations offset one another.
Once again, the fictitious SushiFresh GmbH serves as the running example: a regional producer of fresh sushi boxes in the Rhine-Main area that supplies six supermarket stores in Wiesbaden, Mainz, Frankfurt, Rüsselsheim, Darmstadt and Offenbach every day. Chapter 6 ended with an open question: the warehouse location problem recommended a central site in Raunheim, but left open whether a second site should be added – the cost differences were small, and one important effect remained unaccounted for: the inventories that must be held to protect against demand fluctuations. This chapter picks up exactly there. It asks how large the safety stock turns out to be with central supply from a central kitchen in Raunheim – and how much it differs from the case in which each store plans its own replenishment independently.
The common thread of this chapter can be summarised in three steps. First, we clarify where uncertainty comes from and how it can be classified systematically (implied uncertainty). Next, we show how uncertainty can be buffered quantitatively — via safety stocks that are linked to a desired service level. And finally, the actual core topic is developed: how can the buffer required for this be reduced without lowering the service level? The answer — pooling — is worked through using two structurally related but economically different examples: production capacities (SushiFresh’s pilot phase, in which two kitchens flexibly stand in for each other) and inventories (the six stores which, following the centralisation decision from Chapter 6, are now supplied from a shared plant). In the end, both applications lead to the same mathematical structure, which culminates in the square-root law of pooling.
